Kernel methods are widely used in various Bayesians frameworks and machine learning models for smoothing and density estimation tasks. Although there are existing approaches like Random Fourier Features that efficiently approximate kernel matrices, their accuracy is limited by the number of transformed features and compromises computation time for higher values. This study introduces an innovative set of features that closely match the exponential kernel, eliminating the trade-off between approximation quality and runtime, thanks to the random nature of the features. We experiment with both hand-crafted and automatically generated features, resulting in performance outcomes surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods in multiple evaluation scenarios.

In our study, we successfully demonstrated that any group with a specific transitive action can be seamlessly incorporated into the wreath product, maintaining a matching degree of transitivity. 
Building on this success, we further achieved the same result for restricted groups under primitive actions.
To attain these outcomes, we developed a innovative strategy to simplify complex problems by breaking down their Cartesian components.
Moreover, our approach enabled us to derive a beneficially simple expression for the image of the group in question within the wreath product.

This research investigates the restriction of the Möbius structure flexion problem on conformally flat hypersurfaces of constant scalar curvature in hyperspheres. We demonstrate that for a conformally flat hypersurface of constant scalar curvature, the Möbius structure flexion is equivalent to the equivalence of conformal structures, thereby extending a previous result by Xin to cases where the Weyl tensor is non-vanishing. Furthermore, we establish that any hypersurface of $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ that is conformally equivalent to the standard product is diffeomorphic to either a standard sphere or a hypersurface of the hypersphere that is conformally equivalent to the hypersurface of the standard product.

Optimally planning surgery for complex congenital heart diseases requires an extensive evaluation of heart function and surrounding vascular structures using various imaging techniques. Although patients with these conditions can experience severe symptoms or life-threatening complications, there is still a lack of comprehensive magnetic resonance (MR) image datasets for planning cardiac surgery. Furthermore, heart abnormalities seen in these patients can complicate computer-assisted image analysis methods, making them unreliable for this purpose. By assessing current machine learning-based image analysis methods available for congenital heart diseases, this study highlights key challenges and available solutions. Furthermore, it investigates applying methods designed for common heart conditions to these patients and compares results for heart chambers and major vessels using data from patients with tetralogy of Fallot, showing that this approach can provide accurate results for some structures but not others. Lastly, it emphasizes the critical need for specialized machine learning models that take into account specific heart anomalies and can utilize prior medical knowledge during the planning process to improve overall outcomes.

The performance of computational methods using material simulations depends heavily on how accurately the rate of change of the material properties within each individual element.  This paper examines the advantages and limitations of using a finite element approach to property assignment, and presents outcomes from a study on its application in simulating complex, heterogeneous materials.  Findings show that despite certain constraints, this method can yield significant improvements in both performance and accuracy for a variety of materials.  In some cases, we observed up to a hundred-fold gain in performance, along with up to a ten-fold reduction in errors compared to traditional methods.  In addition, we found that more accurate results could sometimes be achieved with as little as a hundred thousand CPU hours.  In contrast, simulating certain complex materials was made feasible for the first time with our approach, including a biocomposite and certain types of concrete.  We also found that for some materials, computational methods could be made substantially more efficient.  For example, we were able to achieve a comparable level of accuracy with significantly fewer samples when using our method to evaluate the reliability of complex materials, especially those that have never been tested before.  In some cases, we used as little as twenty-five samples to achieve a level of accuracy comparable to but much faster than previous studies that had used much larger sample sizes.  In one case, we were able to achieve a comparable level of accuracy with much shorter computational time when evaluating the compression strength of concrete with various types of aggregate, using only

A wireless communication system that utilizes SWIPT, where a single base station provides data to uplink users and allocates remaining energy for their inference, faces a challenge in optimizing performance. This leads to a robust resource allocation problem that takes into account QoS constraints for information transfer and error rates. The difficulty of this problem is compounded by the non-convex nature of energy harvesting and matrix inversion operations. To address this, we propose an efficient algorithm for finding feasible solutions and optimizing energy, followed by an iterative method to improve solutions under stricter constraints. The effectiveness of these algorithms is demonstrated numerically for various network scenarios.

Integrating all-object detection meta-information into explicit visualization can enhance human understanding of object interactions and guide search processes, ultimately improving decision-making. Introducing the Touching All Objects (TAO) data format, this work introduces a standard for encoding all-object information and introduces the Intuitive Interactive Visualizer (TAIV), a tool that produces an interactive 3D representation of vehicle scenes, integrating metadata on object contacts, speeds, and positions. TAOIV produces immersive experiences and clear graphical dashboards for real-time monitoring and analysis. Furthermore, introducing the concept of Human-in-the-Love (HILO) evaluation, this work provides a comprehensive metric for assessing all-object meta-information through a combination of difficulty, performance, and preference scoring.

Complex systems can be effectively analyzed by examining their rare events through extreme values in a conditionally specified framework. This approach has been particularly useful in studying storms, floods, and other disasters, as well as in financial conditions. Recent research on this topic has highlighted the significance of characterizing conditions using two key features: their extremal nature and their ability to be modeled. A novel theory proposes that complex systems exhibit implicit conditions that are extremal in nature, shaping the system's behavior and influencing its outcomes. This theory suggests that the concept of extreme conditions, which had previously gone unexamined, is fundamental to understanding and modeling complex systems across nature.

This paper aims to improve upon the Baseline-5 (Base-5) model from Huang et al.'s Research on Word Sense Disambiguation Using Glosses (RWWSD) by incorporating the advanced model GlossBERT introduced in the same research. We replace the Base-5 model with GlossBERT to establish a new benchmark for Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). Furthermore, we investigate whether combining BERT-based models can further enhance performance, resulting in the creation of a novel approach called Dual-BERT. This innovative method integrates knowledge from Wikipedia and paper dictionaries, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.6074 on the SemEval-2013 Task 8 dataset, outperforming the previous benchmark.

A kitting system that combines multimedia instructions with corresponding components helps begin to overcame the challenges associated with assembling complex objects from assembly manuals. In contrast to existing research primarily focusing on linear assembly tasks, many objects require sequencing-independent assemblies characterized by the absence of strict task dependencies and the presence of localized interactions. Building on this research, we propose the concept of multimodal procedural programming and present the MultiGuidebook Dataset, which contains over 100,000 printed guidebook pages and more than 1,500 video examples from actual users of the system that can be utilized to train this system by sequencing the guidebook pages and feedback from users to identify any ambiguities arising from incorrect sequencing.

Network dynamical processes are often categorized as typical or atypical based on their symmetry and resulting uniformity. Processes on scale-free networks, which exhibit non-uniform degree distributions and inherent asymmetry, are more prone to generate large-scale effects from minor initial perturbations. This paper delves into the mechanism behind these effects by examining a binary tree network, where a perturbation-induced process is thoroughly analyzed through both theoretical and numerical means. Discoveries reveal that, in the asymptotic regime, the process's outcome is governed by a dynamic balance between the mean and variance of the underlying noise, which arises from the square-root law of large numbers. This finding is significant as it provides a more comprehensive understanding of the effects of noise on network dynamics, superseding previous explanations that solely focused on the influence of network topology.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a related family of polynomials with a generalized weight from the Laguerre type, incorporating similar properties.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is limited by quantum noise in power recycling and the detector's ability to filter certain frequencies. New concepts for enhancing sensitivity at these frequencies include the multi-mode operation of the detector and the implementation of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer. By using the same power recycling cavity for rotating light modes at different frequencies, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer improves sensitivity without the need for a separate beam splitter, which can introduce unwanted light leakage. 

We have modified the standard models for the radio frequency and the quantum noise of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, creating a unified approach that allows for more accurate simulation of the detector's performance. By representing the interaction between the recycling cavity and the main interferometer with an equivalent circuit, we can more easily simulate the quantum noise of the system. 

Our analysis indicates that the sloshing Sagnac interferometer can achieve similar or better sensitivity to the multi-mode operation of the detector, depending on the specific configuration of the system and the settings of the detector's beam splitter.

Next-generation cellular systems are predicted to utilize intelligent surface and large-scale MIMO (XS-MIMO) technologies to significantly enhance total capacity and improve edge user performance in downlink communications. However, due to random deployment of BSs in XS-MIMO architectures, some cellular users may find themselves within regions inaccessible to any BS. In this paper, a new metric called non-intersecting visibility region (NVR) probability is introduced to quantify the proportion of DE regions. A simulation is designed and conducted to investigate the NVR prob-ability in relation to various surface node density and BS deployment parameters. The simulation results reveal that NVR probability increases as the number of BSs decreases or as the density of surface nodes increases. In particular, when the ratio of the number of surface nodes to the number of BSs drops below 10, noticeable NVR regions may emerge. In conclusion, careful planning and optimization of BS deployment can prevent users from falling into NVR regions. Furthermore, the NVR issue can be addressed through appropriate BS deployment strategies.

Building on previous research, our analysis focuses on how gravitational shear instability affects a disk's structure, particularly in terms of substructure formation and evolution. Using three-dimensional radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations that incorporate the characteristics of molecular dust, we forecast how dust structures within accretion disks will behave and evolve, assuming initial conditions where the temperature profiles in these structures follow a specific pattern.

A theoretical model called the big apple model (BAM) is proposed within the relativistic mean field framework to simultaneously explain the rich structure of atomic nuclei and the properties of neutron stars. This model incorporates a relativistic mean field with a fixed isoscalar scalar mean and considers the effects of the BAML and BAMF interactions. It is demonstrated that BAM effectively replicates ground state masses, radii, central densities, binding energies, and skewing of nuclear matter. Furthermore, BAM successfully predicts the maximum mass and radius of neutron stars, as well as the tidal deformability observed in gravitational waves produced during mergers. In addition, BAM implies a direct correlation between the maximum mass of neutron stars and their crust's shear modulus.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of certain factors. Specifically, we found that using a linearized version of the energy bands from DFT within DMFT yields disparate results from those of starting with the non-linear bands. Moreover, employing a non-local approximation like the coherent-potential approximation causes our DMFT results to diverge from full DMFT. Crucially, our study reveals that accurate p-d interactions and inclusion of atomic multiplet interactions are vital for obtaining correct DMFT results. In fact, only by accurately representing these factors can our DMFT results match experimental data, including correct crystal field levels, magnetic ordering temperatures, and spectral properties.

This research proposes a new method for achieving precise operations between neutral atoms using the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen model. As the number of atomic participants increases, it becomes crucial to mitigate the adverse effects of atomic motion. We demonstrate that by carefully balancing the motion of multiple atomic elements and adjusting their coupling with a single vibrational mode, we can achieve stable performance regardless of the atom's position. The proposed scheme utilizes two adjacent optical cavities and includes a method to correct for any atomic loss. Furthermore, an experimental validation using two strontium atoms has confirmed that our approach generates nearly perfect entanglement, exceeding 99% fidelity, and also allows for the detection of any loss event.

Recent research has highlighted the potential for structure-specific dynamics within materials, with every component contributing to overall functionality. However, current images of complex matter often fall short in providing a clear picture of its functioning integrity. This research focuses on understanding the structural behavior of perovskites, a key material category with vast applications, particularly in managing structural symmetry. Using high-speed X-ray analysis, researchers successfully captured the movement of atomic structures within perovskites as they moved through different symmetry states. This achievement allows for a clear image of the structural framework at work, which can now be applied to other complex materials to improve our understanding of their complexity.

Lately, researchers have studied the unconventional metallic behavior of certain
iron-based superconductors, focusing on the interactions between their
electrons. To better understand this phenomenon, a comprehensive theoretical model is proposed, combining the electrons' inherent ferimagnetic nature with strong interactions using a non-perturbative approach称为functional renormalization group. This model predicts an intricate phase map, characterized by a highly correlated Dirac metal phase arising from stable density waves at specific Fermi surface nesting vectors. Within this phase, a dynamic, electromagnetic crystal forms, leading to a conductive state that is highly sensitive to external influences and may exhibit a superconducting state. The stability of this phase can be enhanced by an external magnetic field, potentially inducing a superconducting state via a quantum phase transition. To achieve the highly correlated Dirac metal phase, the intrinsic ferimagnetic interactions must overcome the screening effects, modified by the three-body force, acting on the Dirac electrons. Nonetheless, it is predicted that this phase will collapse, yielding competing correlated insulating phases when the screening effects overcome the intrinsic ferimagnetic interactions. To demonstrate the applicability of this theoretical framework, the model is applied to NaCuHO, a新材料 that exhibits intrinsic ferimagnetic correlations and strong screening effects similar to those present in this material.

We have developed a flexible statistical framework for analyzing independent
data that can take on two distinct forms depending on the underlying state
of the sample. Bimodal distributions arise in various contexts, including
research on circadian rhythms, new technologies adoption, new diseases
transmission, and the mechanisms behind bimodal test scores. The proposed
framework features semi-parametric models for unimodal densities, a method
for estimating parameters, an evaluation of consistency and asymptotic
normality, and a method for hypothesis testing. The concept of a bimodal
density is defined through the bimodal rates and proportions, and the proposed
modeling approach is composed of two separate parts, each with an implicit
bimodal rate and proportion. The model's parameters are estimated using a
bimodal likelihood function, and the framework can be expanded to include
bimodal versions of common distribution types. The proposed model's efficacy
is demonstrated via both simulated data and a real-world example involving
plagiarism rates in college essays.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the existing limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction, assuming two conditions met: a six-day data collection period and the ability to remove background noise. If the $NA62\mu +$ experiment achieves these conditions, it could reach the same standard for muon interactions. However, if the actual lepton is a sub-threshold particle, it will change how often the particles are created.

In a setup involving a Sagnac interferometer, anisotropy manifests differently in the spectral shifts of clockwise and counterclockwise optical paths. This effect can be used to differentiate between the Galiilean and the grgical reference frames. Our research focuses on calculating the spectral shift anomalies occurring in a Sagnac interferometer that is relative to the Galiilean reference frame.

This study introduces the concept of parabolic adjoint operators $\partial_\xi f$ for homogeneous polynomials $f$ in multiple variables and positive integers $\xi$. Building on previous work by De Concini and Notari, a specific class of multilinear maps known as Weierstrass sections $w_\xi$ in $T^n \times \mathbb{P}^{m-1}_n$ are defined by expressing any multilinear map in normal form. It is subsequently shown that the Weierstrass sections $w_\xi$ are adjacent to the boundary in the tangent space and compose the smooth stratified space forming the boundary of the compactified space $\mathcal{K}_{m}$ in $\mathbb{P}^{n^2}_n$. A key finding reveals that the Weierstrass sections $w_\xi$ constitute the nilfibre boundary in normal form, reusing the terminology from [15]. Specifically, in type $A$, each Weierstrass section $w_\xi$ represents a distinct, topologically equivalent toric orbifold.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to their ability to handle long dependencies effectively, yet this achievement comes with a significant computational cost, notably high memory requirements and slow processing speeds, especially when dealing with vocabulary v, which needs to be managed efficiently.

This study revisits the underappreciated $n$-gram models and proposes a novel approach that enables these models to compete with their neural counterparts by significantly enhancing their performance through careful use of modern computer architecture, windowing techniques for large backends, and hash mapping.

We then explore combining $n$-gram models with a forward-looking component, similar to a residual learning approach, which allows for fine-tuning of the models for front-end, back-end, or both, using a small front-end vocabulary.

Our experiments on the Wikipedia text generation task, using 8GB of memory, show our hash mapping $5$-gram model surpasses the best existing fullbench CTB with a significant margin, outperforming even the best neural text generation models (GPT-2 345M, T5 Small) in terms of Perplexity (PP) for short-term predictions (w1, w2, w3), outdoing them by up to 7 times in terms of prediction quality.

When integrated with a forward-looking component, our models with a 50k hash mapping also outdo the best existing $n$-gram models (AWP

We've developed a technique to utilize power series in the context of $\mathbb{Q}$-terminal Fano varieties and their associated smooth points, which draws upon the method of geometric Laurent series expansion, a technique first introduced by Ishii and Takagi. Through our method of near-inversion of power series, we've introduced key concepts such as the geometric coefficient map, the geometric Lagrange formula, and the geometric residue map. Specifically, we've established that the composition of the geometric coefficient map and the geometric residue map yields the identity map, which implies that the geometric coefficient map is surjective. As a consequence of this result, we're able to retrieve key information from a power series that represents a $\mathbb{Q}$-terminal Fano variety and their associated smooth points, including the geometric degree, the geometric canonical threshold, and the geometric local degree.

Recent advances in 3D face reconstruction have produced impressive results, yet faces difficult to analyze remain a significant challenge due to profound nonlinear deformations and limited scanning data's diversities. Such difficult faces include difficult-pose heads, expressions, ages and genders that strongly influence pose and the quality of scanning. From this difficult face alignment and reconstruction problem, we introduce a novel approach called SADRNet, which utilizes a self-aligned dual face regression framework that effectively decouples pose-extraction difficulties from nonlinear deformations. This framework comprises two primary components: a coarse alignment network that removes difficult pose-heads and expressions, and a detailed reconstruction face regression module that focuses on accurate pixel-level prediction. The SADRNet achieves excellent performance on the widely used MRNet benchmark, surpassing SADRNet by 0.87 NCC and 0.009 mm RMSDE metrics.

We've developed novel spin-polarized field theories that effectively describe the breaking of galilean symmetry in motion, leading to a substantial reduction in the number of variables required, an advantage over the conventional approach where the gravitational field is described by a spin-2 field with many more components. Using our streamlined theories, we found that massive gravitons give rise to a particular type of nonmobile particle, called a "fracton," which we also present in the context of broken galilean symmetry. Furthermore, we observe that the conventional massive graviton theory can be mirrored by an expanded model that incorporates a "motional" gravitational field, which we find results in the "fracton" being fully localized.

In this study, we explore an alternative in $\alpha$-attractor inflation models where the classical behavior of light modes is disrupted, leading to a significant increase in their amplitude and a consequent formation of black holes. Despite the limitations of the $\delta N$ approach in these scenarios, we directly compare the spectral densities of curvature perturbations before and after breakdown, thereby bypassing its constraints. We discover that Black Hole formation occurs when the parameter $g$ falls below a specific threshold, and we investigate how the initial and final phases of inflation impact the density of formed Black holes, as well as the ability of sub-solar mass Black Holes to explain the properties of gamma-ray bursts attributed to dark matter annihilations. Given current constraints, we find that the $f_{\ast}/M_{\Pl}$ ratio in these models is best matched by Black Holes with masses around $10^{-7} \ solar \ mass$.

Researchers have recently focused on various properties of marked ordered trees, which consist of nodes and edges, including immediate predecessors and immediate successors. A concept known as "deepest vertices" is introduced, along with an examination of the distribution of this property among all marked ordered trees with a specified number of nodes. A recursively defined generating function allows for the calculation of average values of marked ordered trees' deepest vertices, and some related results can be expressed combinatorially. A key equation for determining the distribution of deepest vertices is established, as well as its conditional average values given a specific number of immediate successors, which can also be estimated numerically. Numerical estimates reveal an intriguing relationship, showing that the average number of deepest vertices closely approximates $n \times 1.2998089\dots$ for large values of $n$.

Election verification systems depend on character recognition technology to confirm the accuracy of election results. To assess this technology's reliability, a new dataset called Informed OCR (iOCR) was created, which pairs the output of character recognition technology with corresponding original scanned images of election ballots. The iOCR dataset comprises several subsets, each consisting of paired data from machine reading results and original image data, along with detailed metadata explaining the processing methodology and source of each subset. The datasets can be used independently or combined to produce quality-assured data suitable for testing and developing ballot analysis systems.

In statistical learning's linear regression linear framework, researchers have investigated the impact of adding unnecessary noise variables (features) on prediction performance when there are significantly more variables than data points available. Recent studies have shown that even when there are significantly more relevant variables needed to understand the data than data points available, the model can still perform well in certain settings like kernel and neural networks. Here we extend this research to a simple, clear set of data points with real values in specific directions and the impact of including extra noise variables in two different models commonly used in time series analysis: the autoregressive model and moving average model. We compare the performance of these models to a dense version of a widely used statistical model and show that the benign effect of including unnecessary variables also applies to the moving average model and its dense version.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper introduces a novel deep learning architecture for speech enhancement. The model employs an asymmetric attention mechanism within a bidirectional framework, utilizing an attention selection layer and a attention fusion layer. Furthermore, a normalisation layer is integrated to address the issue of incompatible feature maps. Two normalisation methods are investigated for optimal performance. Experiments were conducted on the ASR corpus in both clean and noisy conditions. Results show that the proposed model outperforms existing techniques, surpassing the normal bidirectional structure and various unidirectional models with attention mechanisms. Furthermore, the proposed model's performance is comparable to the double RNN structure, yet with significantly fewer parameters.

Music has a universal language that crosses cultural and linguistic barriers,
which is why it's a highly effective means of health education. We've observed
that musicians can effectively use music to disseminate dangerous pathogens,
taking advantage of music's widespread appeal. We call this musicborne
transmission. Throughout history, harmful ideas have been propagated under the
disguise of popular music by certain rappers, but we've seen a beneficial use of
this phenomenon when it comes to public health. We've discovered that a song
lyrically promoting safe blood transmission precautions can experience
exponential popularity, reaching millions of listeners and generating thousands
of downloads, which far surpasses the reach of conventional public health
methods. We suggest utilizing music more extensively for health communication,
potentially recruiting a specific group of musicians to spread vital health
messages.

In various sectors like energy and blockchain, data storage is often overlooked despite being a crucial and underutilized resource. The act of allocating storage carries inherent risks pertaining to both financial return and safety. The primary objective of this study is to mathematically formulate the process of optimal storage allocation in a risk-aware framework, ultimately aiming to establish a connection between risk preferences and desired storage allocation in a decentralized environment. The proposed approach involves applying mean-variance optimization principles to a stochastic asset return model, and utilizing a Value-at-Risk (VaR) mean absolute deviation function to accommodate the concept of risk in a broadly applicable way. The successful implementation of this approach is demonstrated through the use of a real-world dataset from the Ethereum blockchain, where investors can allocate funds to storage services offered by the Protocol for Reliability and Deliverability system and choose between conservative and non-conservative options.

In this research, an intensive examination of the electron dynamics during Auger-Meitner decay is carried out using a time-dependent theory of the process. A finely tuned theoretical approach allows us to accurately model the interaction between core electrons and infrared light in the dipole approximation. By applying this approach in a real space, we can non-perturbatively simulate the process and provide a universal solution, validated by experimental data from R. Pazourek et. al., for any incident laser photon energy. The results reveal a general mechanism driving the ultrafast decay, regardless of specific atomic details. Furthermore, our findings deepen the understanding of how plasma conditions affect the decay rates. By analyzing the emitted XUV photons, we can investigate the electron distribution and identify a separation between high and low energy components within the plasma.

A simplified globe is used to investigate various circulation patterns in terrestrial atmospheres by selectively altering global circulation models' components. This investigation focuses on identifying key mechanisms that regulate and balance atmospheric circulations. The models are modified by gradually changing conditions at the globe's surface and upper atmosphere, as well as by altering the atmosphere's depth. The modeled globe has no rotation, expansive atmospheric conditions allow for the creation of terrestrial atmospheres with geostrophic turbulence. A moderately confined atmosphere is modeled on a globe of standard size, where Coriolis forces balance atmospheric conditions. The model of a tightly confined atmosphere on an expansive globe is also explored. The results are visualized through heat maps of atmospheric conditions, showing how circulations change on different globe sizes. The model of a terrestrial atmosphere featuring jet streams, multiple Hadley cells, and planet-wide atmospheric currents can be observed. Furthermore, the model predicts jet stream locations based on specific dynamics and balances on different globe sizes. The model of two atmospheres on different globe sizes shows similarities and contrasts with observations of gas giant planets.

Most profound changes in deep learning have been  prelude by positive transfer learning experiences.  However, as models become more sophisticated, their initial success begins to mislead by hiding the model's growing vulnerability to variations in data distribution.  Generally, algorithms that personalize models are either ineffective at a large scale, require labeled data for test sets, significantly slow down updates, or fail to account for shifts in data distribution in both directions.  We introduce Datasets for Continuous and Large-scale Updates (DCLU) to broaden the evaluation of adaptive algorithms.  Comprising one billion images and encompassing various levels of shift, DCLU encompasses the largest collection of annotated images used for online learning.  As a result of utilizing the DCLU benchmark, we discover that no learning algorithm can effectively update models in response to shifts in data distribution without human-assisted data collection, without compromising model performance.

We provide novel analytical and geometrical aspects of the generalized algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue for a linear operator. Multiple definitions of the generalized algebraic multiplicity exist, but none have a comprehensive theoretical framework. We propose a new characterization that aligns with a key property and allows derivation of a key identity. This characterization leads to novel results for linear operators, including a connection with a related generalized index. We explore both analytical and geometrical generalizations of the algebraic multiplicity and derive a novel inequality for normal generalized indices. These developments enable a unified understanding of various algebraic multiplicities and provide insights into their interrelations. Specifically, we show how different algebraic multiplicities can be expressed in terms of a new concept, and we derive geometric index formulas that satisfy crucial inequalities. These results have far-reaching implications, including a unified approach to computing algebraic multiplicities for operators that satisfy certain equations, and we demonstrate this approach with computations for a matrix A.

We utilize a population of dipoles, such as alkali atoms, that are coupled to a cavity and exhibit pairwise excitations. This occurs through an optical field that is measured in the sidebands of the dipole transition. The detection process provides a precise benchmark for comparing different types of noise, including virtual two-level system noise. We demonstrate that a specific initial state with pairwise excitations can be employed to accurately measure optical phase shifts. Furthermore, quantum correlations within the ensemble are shown to provide an advantage over classical states in achieving this optical phase measurement. Notably, our approach also allows for the generation of squeezing in the atomic ensemble, which could be used to aid in this type of measurement.

This research provides complete configuration interaction calculations for a set of silicon donor electrons and their spin-coupling considerations across all four silicon valleys. The calculations take into account the central field and exchange integrals through a multi-valley effective mass theory, across distances from 2 to 12 Angstroms. The studies were applied to neutral and negatively charged silicon-29 donors and general silicon donors, and their results are readily usable in the analysis of quantum chemistry and magnetic resonance data from electron spin resonance, central field, and two-body exchange integrals. The length-dependent behavior of the direct and indirect Baumbach and Hopfengärtner type exchange integrals is explicitly demonstrated.

Researchers investigated the quantum conduction properties of HgTe quantum wells that are missing a energy gap, where the Dirac quantum well occurs at the center of a specific energy range. Experimental data collected showed that the conduction behavior is dominated by both Dirac and Landau eddies, located on either side of the Dirac point. A key finding was that the position of the Landau eddies can be predicted by utilizing group velocity instead of energy. Furthermore, experiments revealed an alternating pattern in the eddies' interference at the Dirac point, linked to the quantum Hall eddies' behavior observed in graphene, which serves as a powerful tool for further research.

Intelligent vehicles are expected to be cooperative in order to prevent road accidents, a concept we call Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems (C-ITS). At road junctions, a type of power-saving NOMA protocol can be used, where stronger vehicle signals are turned off. However, this approach may compromise safety due to the exclusion of these vehicles from the communication. A more complex, adaptive two-tier NOMA protocol was developed to balance efficient spectrum use and safety concerns. This new protocol selectively excludes vehicles based on their signal strength and proximity to the base station, and provides communication opportunities to the remaining vehicles. The difficulty of this protocol increases at road junctions because of the varying signal strengths of the vehicles, which can be reflected in the big-Small Gamma variate distribution. Through simulation, the performance of this protocol was evaluated in terms of outage probability and throughput, and the advantages it offers over the original power-saving NOMA protocol were demonstrated.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can adjust their uplink and downlink configurations independently, in response to varying traffic conditions. This per-cell flexibility, while beneficial, if unsynchronized, generates excessive interference known as the 'near-far effect'. To tackle this challenge, we've developed a novel game-theoretic approach that is adaptable to changing traffic conditions and eliminates the need for neighboring cell information. In evaluations, our solution significantly reduces interference levels, resulting in substantial performance enhancements for both interference-free and scenarios that include the near-far effect, particularly without sacrificing essential efficiency.

In the three-dimensional Ising universality class, we've discovered a new way to calculate critical values for order parameter, magnetization density, and the critical point where phase transition occurs, by creating and using a new set of equations that relate these values to each other in an self-consistent way. We demonstrated that at least one set of fixed points exists within our equations and compared the results of our methods to established data from experiments and simulations, finding close agreement and showing our methods can achieve accurate precision with relatively low computational effort. Furthermore, we observed that our methods converge at increasingly tighter points as we raise the number of considerations, implying our equations can also provide accurate solutions for systems not at critical points.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in a subfactor of finite index, is provided. This characterization confirms that a specific condition is sufficient to classify such squares, and as a result, a recent finding by the first author and K. Takeuchi is verified, demonstrating that a subfactor associated with such a square possesses a finite-dimensional Drinfeld double of its unitary group.

Deep learning has been adapted to differential equations through Hamiltonian Neural Networks, which are equations of third order. Despite their success in fitting data, this approach may not be optimal. A simpler method could involve fitting the equations of second order, i.e., the Hamiltonian and derivative functions separately. This method was demonstrated with a case study involving the Lorentz system, which yielded equivalent results to the HNN approach, but with more accurate results for the system's trajectories. Further applications were tested on toy models representing rigid rotors, exoplanets, and multiple planetary systems, as well as a real-world dataset from a physical laboratory, confirming that our method is more efficient and robust than the existing HNN approach. Additionally, this method was found to be less prone to encountering local minima.

Our work brings back the valuable contribution of human input to machine learning systems, specifically their ability to design and build systems that can be relied upon. 
We create a statistical measure, the trust score, that evaluates the reliability of machine learning predictions and enables the system to identify unpredictable patterns. 
Visualizing this score as color-coded options, the score becomes a guide for human interaction with the system. 
Visualizing this score can motivate the human user to focus on regions of feature space where the system is less reliable. 
Using a score that reflects reliability and targeting less reliable areas, we develop a method for gathering data that a system can use to enhance its ability to be relied upon. 
In our study, we combine this approach with human input to improve the trustworthiness of machine learning predictions, found that people can consistently focus on the score and use it to guide their interaction with the system. 
When used as a guide for data collection, the system can be used to improve the reliability of machine learning predictions. 
In our study, we found that a method targeting the score can lead to significant improvements in reliability, even when the data is collected without supervision. 
In our study, we designed and executed an actual system that targets the score and used it to gather data that a system can use to rely more on machine learning predictions. 
In our study, we used the score to guide the interaction of human users with the system and used it to improve the reliability of machine learning predictions.

In security inspections, identifying forbidden items from limited sets of items is crucial for preventing dangerous substances from passing checkpoints.  While extensive research has been conducted on this issue, the quality and quantity of available datasets are generally insufficient, resulting in inferior performance in actual security inspections.  A new dataset has been created to address this issue, called Lateral Inhibition Module (LIMo), which features 16,800 labeled images in 30 different categories and encompasses a wide range of prohibited item types, including electronics, weapons, drugs, and perishable goods, with varied background settings, lighting conditions, and clothing options.  To tackle the challenge of limited visibility in security inspections, a lateral inhibition module has been developed, which effectively reduces false positives and enhances overall performance.  Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of LIMo, achieving comparable or better results than other methods.  The dataset and the module are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Qianzengxia/LIMo.

We introduce a new polynomial, $\mathcal{Z}$, for oriented links in a specific topological space, $T^2 \times I$. This polynomial has the ability to distinguish between different links, is sensitive to the sliding of links, and appears to align with the volume hypothesis of topological quantum field field theories. The construction of $\mathcal{Z}$ employs a path integral approach using a $U(1)$ TQFT on the "thickened knot diagram graph", incorporating special edges and a insertion of the R-matrix.
