which reflects both the semantic information surrounding a target word and its 
properties.   imperfect WSD evaluation protocols often use only a limited set of 
context words, typically close to the target word, to form the context-gloss input. 
This evaluation method is flawed as it discards extensive extra semantic 
information that could be obtained by expanding the WSD context.  In this study, 
we propose enhancing WSD through context enrichment.  Specifically, we suggest 
augmenting the WSD context by incorporating additional words that are similar to 
the target word.  We develop two context expansion strategies, BA-WSD and RT-WSD, 
to be applied to textual semantics extraction techniques like BERT.  Our results 
demonstrate that context enrichment can significantly improve WSD performance, 
yielding substantial gains in accuracy when evaluating polysemous words on the 
Multi2k corpus.  The context expansion approach also proves beneficial for 
WSD tasks involving monosemous words.  Furthermore, deeper analysis reveals 
that the expanded WSD context preserves the original meaning of the target word, 
thereby aiding in the process of sense disambiguation.

This study defines a new class of operators that can be represented as a sum of modified modified integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function, in relation to the regularisation of the standard integral representation of the reciprocal gamma function. A connection is also established with the original expression of the reciprocal gamma function.

In our research, we demonstrate the capacity to identify the top quark, specifically, in interactions between proton and heavy ion such as lead or xenon. Leveraging existing datasets and analyses, we essentially reveal the feasibility of detecting the top quark at the Large Ion Collider within the current technical framework. Furthermore, we anticipate that enhanced top quark production rates will accelerate data collection in areas that are less thoroughly investigated.

This paper introduces a novel end-to-end interpretation model for both single and nested SQL tasks. Our approach involves a cross-domain text-to-SQL model that can handle various database schemas, along with a proposed auxiliary task to aid the model in generating accurate parse trees while also addressing the imbalance issue in data. Using a publicly available dataset, we conducted five different experiments, including splits and newly created datasets. Our results show substantial improvements in accuracy, particularly for nested queries, when using our proposed model compared to state-of-the-art baselines and models trained separately for in-domain and test-set evaluations.

This paper delves into the application of differential privacy within network graph structures.
It should be noted that the literature in this domain is fragmented and scattered.
To address this issue, we have compiled the existing bodies of work on differential privacy in network graphs, focusing on various tasks such as node and node attribute hiding, graph topology privacy, query answering, node classification, and data utility in these domains.
In addition, we outline the different methods employed to achieve differential privacy in these scenarios,
and where possible, we present comparative DP-parameter results.
We have also identified open problems for future researchers in this field.

The vast amount of data that Euclid will generate will significantly impact our understanding of cosmology and astrophysics in the coming decade. This presentation will summarize the impacts of Euclid on dark energy research, black hole dynamics, the development of deep wide-field surveys, and the creation of morphological catalogues. Furthermore, it will highlight how existing techniques and infrastructure for analyzing Euclid science will leave a lasting legacy beyond the project's conclusion.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping systems in challenging driving conditions. Our approach uses a combination of complex road patterns and a search process to find dangerous intersections, cul-de-sacs and narrow bridges. Through simulations, our method demonstrated the ability to test how well an ALKS system can navigate difficult paths, as well as provide insight into system limitations. Additionally, our results indicate that searching for difficult configurations can be an NP-hard problem, and we explore the implications this has on road safety.

To encourage casual exploration of music, music playlists are frequently used.
Effective music playlists should include detailed descriptions that convey the content and mood of the tracks.
While creating such descriptions is straightforward for a small number of tracks with human assistance, manually crafting them becomes impractical as the number of tracks increases.
To encourage the widespread adoption of music descriptions, this research aims to explore the potential of automatically generating narratives for music playlists using advanced techniques.
In this study, we propose novel approaches to this challenge by leveraging the sequential nature of both the lyrics and the structure of the songs.
Experimental evidence demonstrates the effectiveness of our methods over existing baseline models.
Furthermore, visual examples illustrate the potential of our best-performing method to produce high-quality music descriptions that capture the mood and flow of the songs.

A new hydrodynamic model, called random quantum hydrodynamics, has been developed to incorporate quantum fluctuations in interacting boson systems through a stochastic Hohenberg-Beerman equation. The model's accuracy has been verified by comparing its predictions for quantum fluctuations with those of a quantum many-body theory and Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, applying this model to uniformly distributed quantum gases yielded a pressure that perfectly matches the established Thomas-Fermi approximation.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in precise boundary localization, particularly at the action boundaries. To address this issue, we propose a solution called Dual Context Aggregation Network, or DCAN, which enriches the feature representations of individual video frames by incorporating information from surrounding frames. In DCAN, adjacent frames are considered to have smoother context, while distant frames provide complementary semantic information that may be lacking in certain features. Integrating both types of context is done through an innovative dual aggregation module that adapts features from multiple scales effectively. Additionally, this DCAN architecture can also be applied to other single-shot action detection methods without requiring any modifications to their loss functions or detection protocols. DCAN achieves a remarkable boundary improvement of 12.7 points and becomes the top-performing method at AWA10 and MSRA-Action benchmarks.

The long-lived, rational-spectrum internal transport barriers found in ion temperature gradient modes are contrasted with the non-rational spectrum palm tree modes discovered in the JET tokamak. A detailed analysis of the palm tree modes' properties using JET data has been performed, and through linear and nonlinear gyrokinetic simulations, the origin of these unusual ion internal transport barriers has been investigated. It was found that the palm tree modes exhibit a similar electron heat barrier to ion heat barrier seen in IEG modes, arise from a nonlinear, local mode at the plasma edge interior, and are distinct from global TEM modes due to their distinct spectrum and spatial structure. However, they share a similar driving force with the latter, contrary to the former. Furthermore, the palm tree mode's localized structure prevents it from influencing central electron temperature. As such, these unusual internal transport barriers are being compared with the traditional ion internal transport barriers found in JET and present challenges for future devices like JET upgrade and JT-60U.

This research focuses on resolving collisions between mobile robots in a two-dimensional space through an innovative approach called the Dynamic Vortex Potential Field (DVVPF). Unlike traditional methods, the DVVPF allows for a more flexible representation of the environment, as the virtual forces can be easily adjusted to prevent collisions based on the relative positions and movements of the robots. A significant advantage of the DVVPF over the original Vortex Potential Field (VPF) method is its enhanced capability to handle complex scenarios involving multiple robots moving in various directions, even when the line of movement changes, by effectively identifying and avoiding unstable equilibrium points. Furthermore, the DVVPF method exhibits superior performance in handling stable equilibrium points under certain conditions, as well as improved convergence to desired convergence points with reduced final velocity. Empirical results from simulations and real-world applications demonstrate the effectiveness of the DVVPF method in achieving smooth, efficient, and stable equilibrium and convergence for the line of movement of mobile robots.

Given the generation of random letters following a Markov process and an associated cost for each letter, our study investigates how likely it is for a sequence of $n$ generated letters to have a significantly lower cumulative cost than expected. Under both absolute and relative entropy metrics, we mathematically demonstrate that the probability of this unusual event declines exponentially with $n$, and that the most common way this unusual scenario unfolds involves dividing the sequence into segments, each generated through a different perturbed Markov process and then concatenated together. Furthermore, the overall probability of this lower-cost occurrence is shown to be dictated by the most efficient such partitioning scheme, where efficiency is measured in terms of the product of each segment's likelihood and cost. Lastly, our study reveals that this principle becomes particularly clear when the Markov process is made up of independent components or when it consists of two contrasting Markov processes, each representing an equally likely scenario.

The emergence of wireless sensing through wireless communications technologies has prompted investigation into extending this capability using intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS). A novel concept, IRS-supported radar, has been introduced where an IRS is integrated to support radar systems, enabling target parameter estimation through multi-path signals that have interacted with both the radar and the IRS. A system model for this configuration is presented, and the performance gains of the IRS-supported radar system over the conventional system are analyzed using a large system model. Specifically, under conditions of large radar and IRS antenna counts, it is demonstrated that the standard mean squared error (MSE) estimator can achieve accuracy comparable to the optimal Bayesian estimator (BET). Furthermore, as the system parameters increase, the MSE estimator's performance in the large system regime improves and surpasses its small system counterpart, yielding a significant advantage of approximately 3 dB in bias as illustrated through simulations.

A comparative fuzzing approach is introduced as it combines the advantages of different fuzzers, but currently, there's a lack of established guidelines for contrasting fuzzers due to the method's complexity. We've developed a framework called FuzzEval to evaluate and compare fuzzers, focusing on efficiency, effectiveness, and usability. Within this framework, we applied our evaluation criteria to compare whole-file and incremental fuzzing for adding elements. We discovered that for file formats with widely used features, whole-file adding is more effective, but incremental adding outperforms it in less common scenarios. Additionally, we integrated a result from a previous study by incorporating a location-sensitive strategy in our evaluation of adding, and found it significantly outperformed the basic incremental approach in terms of effective and crash diversity.

Our analysis of the current state of deep learning-based continual learning has been conducted, and the existing approaches have been compared based on their risks of catastrophic interference. We designed a basic baseline for evaluation, and we found that many CL models performed similarly to or barely exceeded this baseline. As such, many state-of-the-art methods may offer only a marginal improvement over random performance, and they risk significantly deteriorating when evaluating on challenging benchmarks. Based on theoretical analysis, a simple mathematical formulation and empirical validation through comprehensive experiments, we've identified a critical condition that needs to be satisfied for any new CL method to be considered effective. This requirement must hold for any potential benchmark, and any new method that fails to meet this standard risks significantly deteriorating when evaluating on challenging benchmarks.

We establish a continuous assignment of regions within a metric space that minimizes a given length criterion across all possible homotopy classes relative to a bounded set, within any space that meets the characterizations of a PN-space. This achievement mirrors a finding by Colding and Minicozzi for topological manifolds in Rn. Additionally, if the metric space is the Euclidean space, we prove that this assignment can be made continuous even with respect to the h-topology. This result extends a finding by Hutchinson in a setting of topological manifolds of finite homotopy type.

A solution $u$ to the semilinear heat equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$ is being studied on the real line, where the nonlinearity $f$ satisfies specific growth conditions. On the real line, the solution's long-term behavior is being examined. Given that a nonlinearity $f$ has compact support, its bounds are defined by two constants $A$ and $B$. If certain integrability conditions are met by $f$ over the interval $(A,B)$, a significant discovery has been made. For any initial condition $v$ between the bounds $A$ and $B$, the solution $u$ will gradually approach a stable equilibrium at negative infinity and an unstable equilibrium at positive infinity as time progresses. Moreover, the rate at which $u$ approaches these equilibria is being demonstrated to be exponential both uniformly and non-uniformly at both ends of the real line. This finding is being proven using a method that involves a novel rescaling of space and time, along with a new, versatile framework for analyzing the heat equation's behavior on the real line. This framework enables a unified approach to understanding various results and proofs about solution dynamics, including those found in existing literature.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus have revealed an unusual phenomenon: multiple nuclear shapes with the same spin value (0+) coexisting at similar energy levels. A key question arises whether the low-lying 0+ states can be attributed to a specific 0+2 state with zero angular momentum, or if it's a result of a unique interaction between nucleons causing a distinction between these states. Researchers tackled this question systematically, starting with a thorough examination of the nuclear single-particle structure using a relativistic model, and subsequently focusing on the coupling of angular momenta among the particles. Additionally, a semi-relativistic shell model was employed to analyze the 0+ states up to 2.46 MeV in detail. The researchers found that the 0+ states could indeed be distinguished by their total angular momentum single-particle interaction, and these findings were further validated through experimental validation.

Provided a continuous function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$, determining the points where $f$ equals zero may be accomplished through either methods of query-based evaluation or finding points directly. We differentiate between these approaches as optimization (directly querying or locating points) and learning (evaluating the output value at points). Our analysis centers on the complexity of learning Lipschitz continuous functions under this distinction. Specifically, we establish the minimal number of evaluations necessary (under various measures) for a specific class of functions characterized by a maximum rate of change, or Lipschitz constant. We prove that for functions with a Lipschitz constant $L$, the necessary number of evaluations grows at a rate of $K\cdot L + K'$, where the evaluation's outcome is influenced by the function's rate of change. Notably, we demonstrate a significant increase in difficulty for functions with higher dimensions when their behavior exceeds that allowed in one-dimensional scenarios. We further investigate the implications of this finding, particularly in the context of reaching equilibria in a class of games with limited rate of change in payoffs. We establish that reaching $\delta$-approximate equilibria in these games requires evaluating the necessary interactions between players at least $O(\frac{n^2}{\delta})$ times.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through task testing and model validation, but the process of hyperparameter optimization can introduce significant variance. This can lead to inconsistent results and ultimately produce suboptimal parameter sets. Studies have revealed that 5-fold cross-validation can generate highly variable outcomes when applied to neural network variance reduction is achieved by employing an even split of training and testing datasets. Building upon this finding, we investigate whether combining CV with independent variance-reducing techniques yields optimal results. Our key innovation introduces the J-K fold nested cross-validation technique, which combines even-split validation and CV to vary training and testing datasets while preserving a balanced proportion. This method allows for the comparison of model performance across different hyperparameter configurations. Our study demonstrates that the J-K fold method significantly reduces performance variance by an order of magnitude, outperforming even-split validation and the original five-fold CV technique. This technique is particularly useful for hyperparameter optimization, as it minimizes the risk of selecting suboptimal parameters due to high variance.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology is highly dependent on high-quality data. To improve the performance of neural networks, self-supervised learning techniques add label-free contextual information from surrounding entries, enabling models to learn representational hierarchies. Contextual information can be divided into global and local contexts. This paper delves into a comprehensive survey of knowledge learning techniques based on self-supervised learning, focusing on enhancing the quality of embedded representations through contextual information handling. The survey covers various aspects including data generation, data quality control, and learning strategies to balance contextual information. A quality equation is proposed to unify this research. Building on this proposal, we classify existing studies and propose a novel instructor-student architecture, consisting of an instructor network that learns an additional auxiliary context and a main learning context. This architecture enables model embeddings to be enhanced by additional context and is recommended for future self-supervised learning techniques.

We introduce a novel, efficient representation method for functions in graphical models, which we call Range-restricted Intervals. This approach offers several advantages, including enhanced readability and computational performance. We demonstrate its effectiveness in the context of Exact Mean-Field Approximation (MFA) for single tasks, where our method results in an approximately 2-fold improvement in computational efficiency, without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, our method is applied to Exact Multi-task Parameter Estimation (MPTE), yielding up to a 5-fold acceleration without accuracy degradation, and also addressing the issue of constraint handling. Our method enables the incorporation of complex constraints, including those related to parameter ranges and external constraints, which is particularly relevant in the context of the latest state-of-the-art methods for multi-task learning, where regularisation is often used to satisfy such constraints.

This research absorbs a specific light pulse at an ultracold atomic cloud of strontium, and our study shows that the data can be accurately interpreted by factoring in the recoil of atoms being scattered by photons, and we re-examine the equations developed by Voigt in 1910 in the context of photon recoil and find they closely resemble the absorption formula first proposed by Lorentz in 1906, and we present the evidence that the form of the recoil-induced line shape observed here is unique and cannot be replicated by any other theoretical model.

The response of suspensions to applied stresses varies significantly, 
with their behavior drastically shifting from fluids capable of supporting large 
shear stresses to solids under shear thickening conditions, used extensively 
in impact-protection systems. Despite this, the transition threshold in terms 
of the stress conditions that trigger this shift has been difficult to measure 
and compare due to the lack of a standard method for applying shear stresses to 
these suspensions. Through a series of experiments, we investigated how the 
properties of these suspensions, characterized by their颗粒体积分数 and viscosities, 
could be understood through the concept of normal stress, prior to and during 
their shear thickening transitions. Further analyses revealed that the 
conditions governing this transition could be met in two distinct ways, 
depending on whether the applied shear stress exceeded a critical value, 
which could be directly related to the suspension's critical gap width. This 
discovery reveals a universal pattern in the shear behavior of these suspensions, 
with significant implications for our understanding of their microstructural 
dynamics.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $R^*(n)$, is identified as a quotient of the two rank algebra. The author demonstrates that this $R^*(n)$ is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through explicit construction, utilizing a partial basis formation. Consequently, the respective centralizer generators can be expressed in terms of the initial $n$ number of creation annihilation operators from a single bosonic mode. By deriving a centralizer relationship, a corresponding graph is defined, and it is proven that the edges within this graph represent fundamental racah operators applicable to any $n$-rank special Racah algebra. Additionally, the connection between this cycle graph and the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_m)$ for any integer $m$ is explored, and a general formula is provided for the degrees of coefficients in these algebras.

Our study shows that in a bilayer honeycomb magnet with D3 symmetry, the twisted superfluid and supersolid phases of triplons can exist when interlayer interactions are strongly antiferromagnetic and exceed the difference in intralayer exchange interactions between the two layers. Using a Superspin-t-supersolid mean-field theory, we show that these twisted phases appear as cross-over points between two kinds of supersonic solids, involving different ordering patterns of D3 symmetric magnets. Our results also reveal that in the twisted phases, triplon condensation and magnetic order coexist, and the expectation value of the supersonic order is made possible by the long-range nature of the D3 symmetric interaction. Furthermore, our study provides insight into how to induce the twisted superfluid and supersolid phases, and may help in identifying them through future experiments that measure the D3 symmetric supersonic order.

This research delves into high-dimensional collisions between dark matter and nuclear targets, investigating how dark matter's incident velocity, the angle of recoil, and other factors influence the collisions' outcomes.

A significant portion of the world relies on search engines for access to a vast array of online information. Despite this dependence, there's little understanding of how algorithmic biases from these platforms affect who has access to different perspectives. This lack of knowledge stems from the difficulty in measuring the impact of search engine recommendations on non-expert users. This research fills that gap by assessing how often participants overlook relevant, opposing viewpoints due to Google's Web search's personalisation algorithm. Results show that many users don't have easy access to search results that align with their preferences and can easily be manipulated into missing significant information. Furthermore, these users are often influenced into adopting the prevailing opinions presented to them.

We are extensively analyzing the sub-Standard-Model features of a novel deep Muon-Particle Collider operating at 10 TeV center-of-energy. We detail how this collider will precisely measure heavy particles, potentially revealing principles governing particle stability and decay. Its capabilities to examine theoretical scenarios like extra dimensions, composite Higgs models, and the composite muon concept are particularly advantageous. The novel design of a 10 TeV Muon-Particle Collider will utilize advanced magnetic technology to achieve a compact 800m ring  earth-sized tunnel, enabling significant scientific investigation into the structure of the Standard-Model.

Building upon our earlier research, this study expands the concepts and applications of motion-corrected 4D (3D+respiration) MRI. Initially demonstrated with a research MRI scanner at low field strength, this technique is now applied using a clinical 1.5T whole-body scanner. To create high-resolution respiratory traces, we utilized a 50cm bellows and analyzed its displacement with 100ms temporal resolution. Patients are scanned in multiple static 2D T2-weighted images, and then combined with their corresponding motion-corrected 4D datasets. As an illustration, this method is used to create a high-resolution internal navigational system (INS) for the abdomen, consisting of a high-resolution respiratory trace and motion-corrected 4D datasets in two approaches: as separate datasets or as a single high-resolution 4D (3D+resp) image using the clinical 1.5T whole-body scanner. By providing enhanced visualization of moving organs during breathing, this method improves surgical navigation, reducing the need for scans under general anesthesia in awake surgeries.

A dynamic system's safe control synthesis through linear constraints is achieved by proposing an Integrated Secured Control (ISCF) barrier function. This innovation enables finding a control that maximizes an objective while guaranteeing the system remains within predefined safe parameters. We prove that the optimal control can be calculated efficiently using an interior point algorithm, which converges to the ISCF's value. A rigorous proof of convergence to a feasible, constrained maximum is provided. Moreover, the algorithm's low complexity of $O(m^3)$ allows for computational applicability. A case study on secure spacecraft rendezvous demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness.

In this paper, we provide new representations of various regions including knowledge, alternative, necessary, sufficient conditions, as well as the objects within an universe using CF-approximation spaces. First, we discuss the fundamental properties of CF-approximation spaces. Then, we provide definitions and characteristics of upper and lower approximation operators associated with these spaces. Next, we examine the basic properties of specialized CF-approximation spaces such as T1-to-3, T4-to-5, and homeomorphic CF-approximation spaces. Finally, we show how the representations of an universe using classical and CF-approximation spaces can be utilized to improve the efficiency of knowledge systems in describing regions of an universe.

The paired-permutation test in regression models has long been utilized but with traditionally cumbersome methods of computing its variance that may lead to inaccurate results. The authors of this paper introduce an innovative approach based on Monte Carlo simulation to accurately estimate the paired-permutation variance, thereby enabling more reliable sample size calculations. The new method is shown through a practical example and analyzed theoretically to demonstrate convergence, allowing for systematic sample size determination.

Lack of comprehensive and organized public shipping sector data hinders the ability of researchers and professionals to conduct in-depth time series analyses of the container shipping industry. To address this limitation, we have created a freely accessible Excel database that includes monthly (or more frequent) time series information on container shipping market variables from 1966 to the present. This dataset includes critical shipping industry data points including container freight rates, shipping volume, new and used container prices, as well as container scrap value data. By providing an easily accessible dataset, we aim to facilitate the conduct of rigorous and repeatable time series research and analysis targeting the container shipping industry.

K. Hasegawa's veering triangulations associated with punctured surfaces offer a
fundamental framework for studying the 3D Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ and its
representations. This note establishes that veering triangulations can be derived
from loom areas, a model used to illustrate the $T_1$-invariance of the scalar product
in $\mathfrak{sl}_3$. Consequently, we provide a method to obtain veering
triangulations from crosspieces in loom areas, thereby proving a specific case of
R. Kosterlitz and J. Shiraishi's conjecture regarding loom areas and 3D $T_1$-invariant
state spaces. This method also yields 3D state spaces with veering triangulations
from loom diagrams including multiple types of crosspieces, making state spaces
more practical for modeling interaction processes. As a result, we are able to
construct veering triangulations on certain 3-manifolds like $S^3$, $S^2\times R$,
$HP^1\times R$, and $SO(4)/U(2)$.

Deep graph neural networks excel at the task of node classification but function as opaque systems, obstructing comprehension of their underlying operations. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that incorporates the principles of node importance from a pre-trained GNN model into the edge-space of a target simplified network. By leveraging the performance of this distilled network and maximum cut maximization of the weighted graph, we can effectively maximize the interpretability and preservation of information in the target network. A particular advantage of this method is its compatibility with the establishment of a clear theoretical basis for edge-space coarsening, which is particularly effective when using non-differentiable objectives. A key innovation of this method is its ability to leverage the powerful non-linear capabilities of GNNs without compromising the clarity of its operations. A theoretical basis for this method is established, and our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in outperforming existing solutions on multiple benchmark datasets, including Cora, PubMed, and Facebook Pages.

The CountSketch algorithm is a basic and highly popular method for approximating frequent elements within a data stream, particularly in cases where the stream is inclined to increase the frequency of certain elements. Unfortunately, earlier analyses of CountSketch assume a probabilistic nature of the data stream, thus excluding adaptive streams. In such adaptive scenarios, hosts can deliberately craft streams designed to baffle or deceive sketching algorithms. Although previous studies have found that basic count sketching fails on such adaptive streams, these studies have found that several enhancements to the algorithm can rebalance the situation. In particular, it was discovered that two fundamental modifications to CountSketch enable it to withstand an infinite inclined data stream. It was also found that, contrary to earlier expectations, utilizing more diverse basis functions does not increase the algorithm's resilience to an inclined stream.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular subsets of a manifold with positive scalar curvature can be diffeomorphically deformed away through a surgery-like process. In Part II, we apply the procedures established in Part I to the removal of singularities found in Gromov-Lawson and Michael-Manning's work on splitting a manifold into pieces with positive scalar curvature, specifically cases where one component exhibits the structure of K3.

A liquid containing magnetic flux tubes shows remarkable similarities to the non-relativistic two-fluid model, despite not having the same fundamental symmetries.  When a specific type of superfluid vortex line interacts with a magnetic flux tube, it leads to a flow that's directly proportional to the flux tube's diffusion, similar to how viscosity works in a fluid.  This relationship becomes relevant when considering the rate at which mobile entropy is produced, which provides a way to describe the Nernst effect in this context.  Furthermore, a theoretical model for a fluid containing these vortex lines and flux tubes can be used to provide a new, more relatable understanding of the critical velocity for a superfluid that's affected by entropy production, as well as an explanation for the existence of a unique, minimal state of entropy production in this fluid.  This occurs when the velocities of the vortex lines and the flux tubes are the same, effectively allowing the fluid to reach a steady state where entropy production is minimized.  This concept can be relatable to the well-known theorem regarding the conservation of flux tubes in a superfluid that contains only vortex lines.

In recent years, the field of optimization-based predictive control has made significant progress, yet there's still room for improvement in real-world applications due to the high computational demands of solving optimization problems at every time step. A less intensive approach known as managing system flexibility has been developed, which identifies the range of feasible control actions within a given flexibility buffer around the optimal control sequence. This paper focuses on enhancing the flexibility prediction method by utilizing historical data to accurately estimate future system behaviors and simplifying flexibility calculations. Furthermore, it explores the use of low computational complexity models for flexibility estimation and demonstrates the effectiveness of our method through simulations on complex scenarios such as electric vehicle grid charging, where the predictive control problem proves intractable with conventional methods.

The growth of high-dimensional data set by the 3rd Generation of Internet is paired
with an increased demand for the 4th Generation of Internet that can filter out
irrelevant data and identify novel information. One of the key applications of
machine learning is in financial forecasting, in particular in predicting stock
values. Ensemble methods that combine multiple models are often more reliable
than individual models, yet current approaches are still struggle with issues of
interpretability and reliability. This research is focused on leveraging the power
of the BERT architecture to predict stock values and is proposed to be replaced by a
perfectionist neural network in a two-phase ensemble method. We tested this
approach on the Google stock data set and found that our method consistently
outperforms leading benchmark models over multiple time periods.

Recent package-based formalism enhancements have taken the task of calculating high-order scattering amplitudes in Quantum Field Theory to new heights. As these techniques advance, there's a need for an equally sophisticated package to handle complex processes involving many particles and higher-loop interactions in theories like QED and QCD. This need has led to the creation of SCATTER, a universal envelope formalism that can simplify such calculations by reducing the vast number of kinematic variables to a more manageable set. This approach has a practical application in efficiently computing QED and QCD corrections for the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) diphoton production process, scattering two colorless scalar particles.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with center of mass energies of 3 TeV and 1 TeV, respectively, by studying their sensitivity to new BSM interactions through EFT frameworks. Our analysis focuses on scalar EFT modifications to the WWHiggs coupling, characterized by the $\kappa_\lambda$ parameter, and evaluates the impact of these interactions on DHiggs cross-sections. Notably, we find that deviations in the $\kappa_\lambda$ parameter can be identified at both colliders through specific final state signatures, particularly the four leptons channel arising from $HH\to (γγ)(λλ)$. We observe that the 3 TeV CLIC detector offers superior sensitivity to EFT operators compared to the 1 TeV ILC. Furthermore, we propose a systematic methodology for incorporating higher order effects within the EFT framework to enhance the comprehensiveness of our analysis.

The structure of a perfect fluid's dynamics is excessively expansive, allowing for non-kinetic models. A non-kinetic model is identified and characterized by restricting model parameters to models that exhibit one or more of the following properties: mass conservation, dismodeling imitativeness, or model simplification. Following this, multiple formulations are explored to discover equivalent models. A unified approach is then established, leading to alternative models, such as models utilizing a singular scalar field, the Fodor-Tseftis scalar, or the Liouville field.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that mimics anti-gravity, allowing for a quicker determination of the resulting entropy when these shocks interact and a slower but accurate measurement of entropy production during their initial phase. A specific model within the framework shows that entropy behaves according to a exponential function of time, while also enabling a more precise assessment of interaction effects between two identical shocks, revealing a significant increase in entropy produced when the shocks interact compared to when they move independently. Furthermore, a diverse range of interaction outcomes can be achieved by altering the relationship between the speeds and sizes of the shocks, and a limitation to the framework's accuracy is discussed.

We investigated the drag forces acting on cylindrical objects as they move lengthwise or crosswise through a granular bed. Uniquely, we examined cases where the cylinder's radius matches its length, creating a 1:1 ratio. The interactions between the cylinder and a depth of three times its length were simulated using the discrete element method, with a static boundary condition and a Grashof number of one million. Our simulation revealed an anisototropy in the drag forces, with crosswise movement experiencing roughly 50% more drag than lengthwise movement. Notably, surface area alone doesn't fully explain this anisotropy in drag forces.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation is regulated by gas outflows. A prominent central outflow is seen in the galaxy, with velocities up to 600km/s and mass ejection rates as high as 10^{-1}M_{\odot}/s. These outflows show a clear connection with local star formation levels but also vary with position across the galaxy. Below a scale of ~1.5kpc, outflows are suppressed, possibly due to magnetic fields channelling gas along the galaxy's spiral arms. Above this scale, the outflows are strong enough to push on the galaxy's rotating gas, creating regions of quiet space where star formation is hindered by the lack of available gas. A simple model, combining this outflow strength with another commonly used model, successfully predicts the galaxy's star formation pattern.

The organization of large-scale systems relies on efficient tuning of many settings. OrganizedBO is an innovative approach that analyzes system logs to identify patterns, eliminating redundant optimization efforts. By representing the solution space as a graph, it allows the optimizer to leverage patterns and avoid repeating work, enhancing the efficiency of the optimization process. To test its effectiveness, we conducted a large-scale experiment on organizing and optimizing a large synthetic dataset, and compared it to the current standard approach, demonstrating significant improvements in efficiency and accuracy.

Our research indicates that triangular flow $v_3$ can effectively be simulated using our transport model, provided the initial geometric triangularity $\epsilon_3$ is properly taken into account. By incorporating this parameter, we discovered that the magnitude of triangular flow is substantially influenced, yet it surprisingly relies little on specific physical properties such as equation of state, shear viscosity to entropy density ratio, or initial entropy density. To understand the relationship between flow and this parameter further, we formed various effective temperatures and determined that $v_3$ has a linear correlation with the triangularity-effective temperature. Furthermore, within the context of triangular flow, we found that the dependence on the initial entropy density can be reformulated as a reliance on the initial radius of the colliding systems. This discovery enables us to predict Au+Au and Cu+Cu flow patterns based on measured $v_3$ in Cu+Cu experiments.

Over the years, the reliability of Web Data has improved, enabling a wide range of applications that involve combining data from multiple, independently managed sources. Nonetheless, several critical issues persist, as no comprehensive quality evaluation system has been established for such datasets. In response, we have developed QuotA, a high-performance quality assessment module for LFOs that leverages logical sampling to efficiently process large datasets. By reducing query evaluations to a series of three boolean checks, we can leverage existing samples from operations like joins. To date, QuotA has been integrated into three different systems, and performance measurements indicate that it can outperform several alternative approaches in terms of both precision and processing time.

The characterization of time series by a set of statistical parameters is a method commonly used in the analysis of dynamic systems. For Gaussian time series, the estimation of these parameters from time series data has proven to be an effective means of both understanding and predicting system behavior. For non-Gaussian time series, a specific parameterization of the cumulative distribution function, known as the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) transformation, allows for the estimation of parameters and the prediction of future values. However, the sensitivity of the estimated parameters to measurement noise has been found to limit their utility in describing dynamic systems. This research introduces modifications to the classical CIR parameter estimation technique, resulting in novel estimators that are less sensitive to measurement noise. These new estimators are evaluated through Monte Carlo experiments for both synthetic time series data and real-world data, showing that they outperform the conventional CIR estimator in terms of effectiveness. Furthermore, the novel estimators are applied to real-world data, demonstrating their superiority over the conventional CIR estimator in terms of goodness of fit.

This study presents a novel visualization technique to capture the spatial distribution and directional patterns of emission lines from active galactic nuclei. We observe that some Seyfert galaxies display asymmetric ionization patterns, with one side showing extended emission and a distinct boundary. Analysis of these regions reveals startled emission, characterized by specific chemical compositions and ionization states. Furthermore, we identify correlated nuclear emission and reflection components, as well as a link between ionization gradients and the morphology of the big broad line region.

As the edge computing environment evolves, assessing computing systems' adaptability to different system-on-chip designs, architectures, and optimization techniques becomes crucial. Traditionally, evaluation methods involve detailed analytical models or simulation tools, yet they are highly resource-intensive and time-consuming. Can we create an efficient, real-world evaluation approach for real systems? Our solution is a real-world, real-system evaluation method named E-DEN, which utilizes actual hardware, actual workloads, and actual operating systems. E-DEN leverages the event-driven nature of applications and systems to minimize the computational and storage costs, facilitating rapid and economically feasible evaluations. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of real systems on actual edge applications by comparing E-DEN's outcomes to those from traditional rate-driven approaches using hardware models. Our experiments demonstrate that E-DEN's evaluations, when matched to simulation results, exhibit excellent E-DEN-to-Simulation and E-DEN-to-Rate-Driven evaluations, with correlations of 0.93 and 0.90, respectively.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved significant breakthroughs in the realms of Beauty physics, including measurements of rare occurrences and rare decays that contradict the predictions of the Standard Model. This study详des the recent findings attained in these areas, encompassing measurements of neutral Beauty meson parameters and results from an extensive search of rare decays and contradictions.

The realistic simulation of autonomous vehicles in complex urban environments remains a significant challenge due to the vast number of possible traffic scenarios. Current methods for testing autonomous vehicles are limited because they can only explore a tiny fraction of potential scenarios, as they rely on manually designing individual scenes. To tackle this issue, researchers have developed ways to modify existing scenes and use data from real-world recordings, though these methods are still constrained and produce results that can distort the natural distribution of traffic elements. To address these limitations, the authors introduced SceneNet, a synthetic dataset containing a diverse range of realistic scenes in urban environments. The data was collected independently for each attribute of the scenes, significantly reducing the number of scenes that need to be created compared to previous methods. They also explored techniques to enhance real-world scene reproduction by adjusting the artificially generated elements, as directly combining components from real recordings often leads to unrealistic results.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find unique periodic Gibbs states associated with certain external fields and temperatures at any level of that tree.

A critical consideration when applying structure-preserving numerical methods to
discretised problems involves ensuring that the associated system matrices have
manageable condition numbers. Otherwise, numerical issues may arise due to
significant inaccuracies in the solution when using standard direct or iterative
solution techniques. This paper investigates the compatibility of preconditioned
Krylov methods with specific algebraic properties of the system matrix. It is
shown that certain matrix structures can hinder the efficiency of commonly used
preconditioners, such as incomplete factorisation, multigrid, and domain
decomposition techniques. As a result, fewer fill-in operations are produced,
resulting in similar complexity and computation costs for successive iterations.
However, this compatibility requirement limits the choice of preconditioners,
effectively restricting feasible options mainly to simple incomplete
factorisation.

Let $f$ be a real-valued function and two sequences $a_n$ and $b_n$ consist of pairs of commuting finitely supported operators acting on a Hilbert space. We establish sufficient conditions for the asymptotic ergodic behavior of the product sequence $f(a_n)b_n$, specifically $\lim_{n\to \infty }{\frac {1}{n}}\sum_{k=1}^nf(a_k)b_kx=y$ if and only if $f(a_n)\to 0$ weakly and $b_n\to 0$ weakly. This result generalizes previous findings related to the individual behaviors of $f(a_n)$ and $b_n$.

We investigate the formation of dust particles in low-metallicity molecular clouds, specifically those with no or very low silicon content. The birth of dust particles is primarily attributed to cooling effects on these clouds. The amount of dust formed depends on the presence of alkaline earth metals like magnesium and calcium, as well as silicon, particularly in regions with relatively high densities. The efficiency of converting total metal content into dust varies significantly, especially in the range of $-2 \leq \log(Z_{\rm met}) \leq -1$. The presence of molecular hydrogen affects the particle growth rate, slowing it down by several orders of magnitude in certain ranges of metallicity. The typical size of formed dust particles is in the range of 0.1 to 0.3 microns, which has important implications for identifying and distinguishing between formed and unformed particles using telescopes, regardless of the metallicity levels. The model is then applied to explain the observed features in supernova spectra, specifically those of supernovae 1998x (Type IIP) and 1954N (Type Ibc). The formation of dust particles in the surrounding environments of these supernovae can lead to increased opacity in their spectra, which can mask their intrinsic properties and potentially classify them incorrectly. The outcome of this process is highly dependent on the distance of the supernovae from the center of their parent galaxies, with closer supernovae more likely to have formed dust particles that mask

Identifying objects in the distance is a crucial ability for autonomous vehicles to interact safely with other road users. Detecting pedestrians and vehicles far ahead is particularly challenging and often overlooked in evaluation metrics like nuScenes. To address this issue, we introduce a new benchmark called Far-Field 3D Detection (Far3Det), which focuses specifically on objects and pedestrians detected in the distance. By filtering the original validation dataset based on detection distance and bird's-eye view position, we provide detailed statistics on the remaining data. Our analysis reveals that missing information far in the distance is heavily concentrated in angular regions that are typically shaded in road maps. Building on existing approaches for distant detection, which often struggle with training data limitations, we propose a evaluation framework and release training labels for the remaining data in specific angular regions to facilitate performance enhancement. Our experiments demonstrate an average improvement of 2.4 meters in detection range using default models, and our results can be viewed in a video demonstration.

The complex landscapes of energy in magnetic systems pose significant challenges in navigating them for the purpose of finding ground states, a task made worse by the local minima that abound. We introduce a novel quantum machine learning approach to determine the ground states of 2D and 3D Heisenberg models, incorporating both spin and long-range interactions. By training a classifier to discern between points near and far from the ground state, it is an unexpected finding that this classifier effectively encodes the ground state itself. Leveraging this, we utilize quantum phase estimation to gradually refine a candidate state until it becomes a ground state, a process accomplished more efficiently than a brute-force approach for certain system sizes. Notably, we are also able to apply this technique to a 3D $L=10$ cube and a 2D triangular lattice with $L$ edge lengths of 12 units. Furthermore, we observe that the critical distance that separates the ground state from the excited state states exhibits an infinite range, declining in proportion to the -1.17th power of the system size.

Non-rigid registration plays a crucial role in aligning medical images for analysis, planning, and monitoring. To ensure accurate results, the model must incorporate both image intensity data and appropriate constraints within a plausible range. Our approach utilizes a data-driven biomechanical model built from CT abdominal organ scans to pre-select regions of interest within a short timeframe. This model's internal forces, externally applied via MRI gradient entropy, facilitate automatic alignment of abdominal organs to the MRI scans within approximately 5 minutes for T1-weighted images. Our fully implicit formulation ensures simultaneous resolution of the mechanical problem and regularization, enabling efficient computation of an energy functional's minima through localized and global optimizations. To avoid unrealistic deformations, the model utilizes a sparse matrix with sparse factorization techniques for efficient computation. Our approach allows for robust and efficient abdominal organ registration, achieving a near-minimal energy state within a reasonable computational timeframe.

This study investigates why self-supervised flow estimation methods struggle with difficult situations such as driving on familiar roads. We hypothesize that these methods have excessive confidence in predictingFlows for difficult scenarios due to their training being rewarded for making an easy prediction even when it's incorrect. A negative influence is observed in the data distribution near difficult samples, which causes these methods to fail. We validate this hypothesis through visual analysis and quantitative evaluation on a real driving dataset. A novel metric learning model is proposed to adapt the difficult samples' training and correct this issue, which shows improved results after being trained. Furthermore, we find that the adversarial training does not overfit and negatively impact performance on reliable samples, opening up possibilities for enhancing difficult samples' prediction through adaptation to their challenging characteristics.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at much lower energy levels, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a novel model that leverages Random Neural Network (RNN) to achieve highly efficient data processing, reducing it by up to 10^5 times when compared to conventional models. Despite the limitations of using simulated spiking neurons that limit real-time performance, we demonstrate the superiority of our model through comprehensive classification tests conducted on the CIFAR-10 and COKE datasets, obtaining classification accuracies of 60.25% and 57.28% respectively.

This research investigates the thermal properties of strange quarks, specifically their pressure, energy density, and speed of sound, within a magnetic field at various temperatures. To account for interactions between quarks, a scalar quark quark interaction is considered within the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) phase. The structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars is then analyzed using the Quark Equation of State (QEOS) derived from the QGP phase. The relationships between stellar mass, radius, and temperature are established for non-interacting quarks, and the effects of the magnetic field on these parameters are assessed. The results show that the inclusion of quark interactions modifies the equilibrium properties of QGP and impacts the characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark stars. Furthermore, the results for non-degenerate quarks are presented.

A specific type of ideal matching, first introduced by Behzadi and universal in nature, is prominently featured in this paper. A graph is considered ideal if it contains a first-type matching that is also a solution to another problem. This focus on ideal matchings is prevalent within the realm of infinite graphs. This study determines the conditions under which a locally finite, infinite graph first defined by Thomassen contains a graph of this ideal nature. Furthermore, a theorem is established: a graph is ideal if it is infinite, 4-acyclic, and satisfies certain conditions regarding its edges. This paper is derived from a more comprehensive analysis of cubic graphs, where graphs are considered ideal if they contain a first-type matching that is also a solution to another problem. Lidl and Panitz introduced the concept of block arrangements in 2003, which provided a fresh viewpoint on classical problems involving irreducible polynomials. We take the discussion further by expanding on block arrangements, introducing new types such as nested and disjoint arrangements. We define nested arrangements formally and explore their connections to irreducible polynomials, including examples of the lowest-degree irreducible examples. We also introduce a new class of nested arrangements called "pairs of Wirsing-type irreducible polynomials" and prove that under specific conditions, these pairs behave similarly to Wirsing's statistical findings. Our research suggests that as the degree of the irreducible polynomials increases, the proportion of irreducible polynomials in this pair of arrangements converges to $1/\varphi$.

This research paper introduces a novel framework called Timeloops for learning and optimizing system call policies in containerized microservices. In the dynamic environment of microservices, maintaining high performance and resource efficiency is crucial. The process of system call policy tuning can be likened to both optimization and reinforcement learning problems. To address these challenges, we propose Timeloops, which combines the strengths of custom-loop and multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches for autonomous system call policy learning and optimization within microservices systems. The primary contributions of our work are the introduction of Timeloops, a framework for autonomous system call policy learning, and the demonstration of its effectiveness through the use of custom agents that can efficiently explore and exploit the solution space, potentially outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while using fewer training resources.

Investigating the Standard Model with an extra $B-L$ symmetry offers a compelling pathway to incorporate multiple new phenomena, including dark matter, while also potentially explaining the small magnitude of neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism. In this paper, a revised version of the $B-L$ extended Standard Model is presented, where the model's parameters are adjusted such that one of the neutrinos remains massless. The in-depth analysis focuses on the possibility of pseudo-Goldstone dark matter, where the $B-L$ symmetry is spontaneously broken, giving rise to a dark photon. The model's viability is assessed through an examination of the dark photon's implications and constraints from direct detection experiments. Under certain conditions, the dark sector could be detected in future experiments such as ADUNE and LEGEND, while the model is found to be in line with current limits on dark matter.

This study develops a point process model for target location that combines grid-based and independent distribution features, utilizing grid cells within specific areas and continuous location probabilities within others. As a result, certain existing grid-based filters become applicable to this new model, streamlining implementation. A specific example is provided where targets are monitored using sensors and tracked via non-linear measurement updates, but are subject to birth, death, and motion dynamics that include an escape mechanism that operates by reversing their course of motion. The development of this new model yields benefits including enhanced target detection through improved grid resolution, yet at the expense of excessive data generation in areas where grid cells are used. A novel application in sensor management is explored where existing grid-based filters are employed to evaluate grid cells' levels of uncertainty and reliability of target detection during data acquisition. This balance is achieved by controlling the proportion of grid cells that are marked during this process. The proposed point process model and its corresponding applications are presented, along with an introduction to a new target model called the "partially grid-based" motion model, which is discussed in detail throughout the study.

This paper studies the null controllability of a one-dimensional population model, consisting of a transport equation with interior control and decay, over a finite time period and spatial domain. We first establish that any initial population distribution can be reduced to zero by an optimal control, thereby establishing reachable sets with controllability properties and proving the null controllability of the population model. The second part of the paper establishes an observability inequality for the associated homogeneous transport equation. We also provide numerical demonstrations of this inequality and present results showing local controllability of the model.

The dynamics of soccer games can remain unchanged despite variations in team compositions, playing surfaces, and game contexts. To cope with this, our objective is to generate robust policies for soccer players using supervised learning in simulation and real-world applications. In scenarios where the ball is unclaimed, teams have the option to perform actions that influence possession. Our approach centers on players' ability to execute actions that increase their team's possession rate, as opposed to merely pursuing the ball. To achieve this, we employ a shape network to efficiently process high-dimensional sensory information and centrally locate the ball. Our tests on a soccer simulation demonstrate that the approach can effectively enhance possession rates through cooperative play.

Time-domain extended source signal inversion has been previously analyzed in frequency-domain studies due to an issue known as temporal aliasing. This effect limits the accuracy of source signal recovery when using broad bandwidth data and requires further investigation. Our initial findings demonstrate that even with limited and discrete frequency data, excellent scan rates can be achieved. This implies that even with a broad frequency step, excellent time-domain signal fidelity can be attained. Under investigation are the impact of frequency step, temporal aliasing, and anti-deconvolution techniques on field and simulated data with known parameters. These studies demonstrate that even with large frequency steps, excellent source signal accuracy can be achieved. This implies that even with data coverage of around 10 percent, excellent source signal accuracy can be expected. These findings have significant cost and data acquisition efficiency benefits.

We demonstrate the generation of optical asymmetry through coherent quantum squeezing in a nonlinear medium. By applying balanced quantum squeezed injections to the side ports of a directional coupler, we have successfully created an imbalance in light transmission between forward and backward directions. Our theoretical analysis utilizes a Heisenberg-Langevin approach to derive the output light's transmittance in both directions. It also reveals that optical asymmetry is directly proportional to the level of quantum squeezing, with more squeezed light resulting in greater asymmetry. Furthermore, the Asymmetry Factor exhibits maximum sensitivity to variations in signal propagation direction, with successful reduction of thermal and vacuum noise through side-band and direct subtraction techniques. By successfully integrating these noise reduction techniques with our method, we have achieved successful operation of the system in both balanced and unbalanced modes.

We present analysis of X-ray data from AstroSat directed observations of the neutron star binary system IGR J19294+1816 during its Type II X-ray outburst in July 2019.  Raising of the binary system's orbital phase is associated with an increase in X-ray emission level.  Low-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations with a amplitude of 1.1 Hz were detected in the power spectrum of the X-ray flux.  These QPOs are typical of low-state activity in this binary system which has exhibited similar behavior during previous high and low state activities in 2015 and 2015.  The system's spectral analysis indicates the presence of a sharp spectral feature at the energy of 21.6 keV.  This feature is most likely a cyclotron line that corresponds to the magnetic field strength of 0.64 x 1013 G.  The detection of Low Frequency QPOs and a cyclotron line during the binary system's high state is unusual and contradicts typical patterns observed in other systems.  However, similar occurrences have been reported in similar systems such as XTE 1918-032 and XTE 1550-564.  These observations provide additional valuable data points that may help to shed light on the underlying physics governing these types of X-ray binaries.

To analyze the long-term behavior of a noisy probabilistic model of an electorical system, where candidates compete for support based on a competition-colonization pattern, is challenging due to the model's stochastic nature. However, by examining the corresponding deterministic model, which applies a mean-field approximation, we can gain insight into possible outcomes, such as species extinction or coexistence, in the noisy system. Through theoretical analysis of the noisy system, we can confirm that these extinction patterns observed in the deterministic model are validated, and we can also explore how the competition-colonization pattern influences the likelihood of certain outcomes, such as the dominant species marginally persisting below its threshold.

Ancient Sundials are timeless instruments utilized for timekeeping, still in practice across the globe, including in Indonesia where traditional sundials serve both practical and artistic purposes. However, the precision of these devices is highly dependent on proper orientation, necessitating a dependable method to record their location and direction. To address this challenge, a web application named Suryakala-Nusantara has been developed to record the details of Indonesian sundials. The application enables the input of relevant data, including the precise coordinates and cultural significance of these timekeeping devices. Through a combination of geospatial visualization and historical context, users can explore and learn about these unique devices, including their founding legends and distinctive features.

This research explores the integration of cognitive reflecting surfaces with D2D communication, potentially solution for mitigating severe signal fading in 5G and beyond systems. We analyze a network where CRS and D2D communications coexist, considering SE maximization and total power consumption minimization as optimization objectives. We develop an efficient algorithm to maximize SE and propose a novel majorization-minimization based algorithm to minimize total power consumption. Simulations demonstrate that the CRS-assisted D2D communication outperforms the integration of traditional reflecting surfaces and D2D communication in SE maximization and total power consumption minimization.

To test the feasibility of using an autonomous LDV system for monitoring hazardous areas, this study presents a setup that allows one person to operate an LDV system far from the measurement location. Consisting of three main components, the system uses a signal generator to link the LDV with a computer, which runs an LDV software package to record and analyze data. By setting up the equipment according to this configuration, the study successfully measured 2D flow fields generated by rotating blades of an autonomous wind tunnel, demonstrating the potential of one operator running an LDV system while another manages the aerodynamic model.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is now being investigated in relation to their usage as an aberration corrector in the transmission electron microscope (TEM). The study determines that slight shifts in phase or position of the plate's influence result in acceptable levels of phase error or spatial incoherence for most practical applications. The study also reveals that the shape of the phase profile is repeatable at various radii without the need for superconduction. The study reveals that replacing the conventional aperture with the phase plate has the potential to mitigate issues of incoherence and beam divergence issues. The study reveals that algorithmic adjustments can compensate for the deviation from the ideal profile. The study has the potential to inform the design of future phase plates and to contribute to the development of advanced TEM techniques.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on pre-trained language representations. However, there's relatively little understanding about whether these representations capture the necessary information for the task when used separately from the training generator. We investigate the encoder components of data-driven dialogue models that generate the responses, gathering both trained generators and non-dialogue models. We evaluate the representations by using a wide range of task-based classifiers and generative networks. Our findings reveal that while certain simple features like topic models and latent semantic analysis perform comparably to an extensive range of generative networks, the representations vary significantly depending on the classifier used. This outcome highlights the entangled nature of representation and generative dialogue models, emphasizing that the model only optimizes for ease of generation rather than clarity or completeness of the encoded information.

Deep learning methods have excelled in image place recognition but LiDAR data comes with additional challenges stemming from its point-cloud nature, resulting in LiDAR place recognition difficulty. To tackle this, previous research combined LiDAR data with images or converted it into scalar maps before applying neural networks. Alternatively, direct deep learning approaches have been proposed, albeit with limited performance due to the vast number of 3D LiDAR channels. In this paper, we introduce a novel direct deep learning network called AttDLNet that efficiently handles raw 3D LiDAR data for LiDAR place recognition. We've incorporated a attention-based channel selection module and a dual-path network to effectively extract features from the LiDAR data. Experimental results show that AttDLOutOutOut place recognition outperforms state-of-the-art direct direct direct direct approaches on two benchmark datasets.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, as live viewer numbers can be unpredictable, providers often rely on cloud computing. By leveraging the cloud's flexibility, they can match computing resources to real-time demand, thus optimizing costs and performance. This research investigates how cloud transcoding performance impacts live video delivery, particularly for events with varying demand patterns. Live live matches were live-streamed using transcoding, evaluated across different setups representative of major public cloud providers. Measurements of latency and reencoding time, as well as throughputs, were collected and analyzed for practical use in cloud provisioning. We developed a flexible performance model for cloud transcoding, which predicts latency, reencoding time, and throughput based on current demand, resulting in reduced provisioning costs for events with fluctuating patterns.

This study calculates non-local screening effects in doped graphene at various temperatures in air, which can be applied to determine the heat capacity and thermal conductance in this material. Non-local screening is calculated using the random phase approximation and its influence on the effective Coulomb interaction is determined. Temperature and doping levels are varied to examine the resulting effective interaction. Using this effective interaction, the thermal conductance, specific heat, and dimensionless coupling constant are estimated within a semi-local approximation. A similar approach is used to calculate the effective interaction in bulk silicon, and its resulting thermal conductance and heat capacity are calculated, comparing the results to experimental data.

Added context is essential for natural language production, as it helps speakers convey information that is not explicitly stated but widely understood.  To test the influence of hiding certain information, this study focuses on a scenario where speakers see both the object being discussed and its location, but listeners only see the object.  A masking strategy was implemented in this study, requiring speakers to ask questions to convey hidden information.  Using the MaskedSpeech system, a study was conducted with participants playing against human opponents.  Results from this study were found to be supported when participants were instructed to act using masking strategies rather than cooperative communication.  hese results also suggested that speakers can learn to communicate effectively even when they are limited by what they can convey.  A model incorporating both masking and limiting information was found to best describe the behaviors of participants under these constrained conditions.

We provide an explicit definition of the spectrum for a specific type of combined system. This system consists of a Klein-Gordon equation, where one end is fixed and the other is connected to an anharmonic oscillator. We then compare the discrete spectrum defined here with that from a study involving the Schr\"odinger equation. In an unrelated part of the research, we use the equation's variational properties to analyze the stability of solutions for a combined system. This system includes a Klein-Gordon equation, with references to an inequality involving the anharmonic oscillator.

Q-ball studies are expanded to include other types of field excitations, as long as they remain confined within the Q-ball itself. The analysis is conducted within a dark sector model that includes a complex scalar and a dark gauge field, characterized by multiple symmetries and a higher-order self-interaction. We find that, despite the presence of higher-order self-interaction, the model can still produce stable BQBs, AQBs, and hybrid AQB-BQBs, with the model's parameters being constrained by these conditions.

The model's parameters were initially set using Milankovic cycles and the Hubble data, with the researchers retaining their approach but focusing on adjusting the parameters within the current universe, considering the constraints of the Hubble data and the model's theoretical limits. 
The Hubble data can be fitted within the model's parameters, with the derived values falling within a specific range, and the model predicting a minimum universe size about 10^-4 times the Planck length. 
However, this minimum size is many orders of magnitude smaller than the minimum universe size predicted by string theory, and considering this constraint, the model requires the Hubble data to be set using the model's parameters, resulting in a specific value, and with this value, the minimum universe size reduces to around 10^-3 times the Planck length. 
The model has also been found to be compatible with a specific type of matter-radiation equality universe time, and with this equality time, the model predicts a minimum universe size about 10^-4 times the Planck length.
