We establish that a sequence of sequences of compact, smooth, disjoint, and uniformly bounded sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ ($n\ge 2$) with uniformly bounded mean curvature satisfies an isoperimetric residue condition if and only if it converges to an optimal configuration under the flat metric after removing a negligible set. The theorem reveals that sets with bounded mean curvature exhibit local $n$-isoperimetric behavior, which can be quantified by an optimal arrangement of $n$ disjoint parts. The description of sequences converging to an optimal $n$-isoperimetric configuration contributes to understanding long-term dynamics of flows, such as the bounded curvature flow.

The model-parallel learning technique is essential for training very deep networks, yet it has significant challenges at the model interfaces. These issues arise due to the need to fine-tune multiple, highly non-linear activation functions simultaneously. A solution to this problem involves applying a novel method called Regional Critic Training (RCT). This method allows for region-specific adjustments to be made by training a separate critic network that is partitioned in the same way as the main model. When applied to practical model-parallel scenarios, RCT is shown to significantly improve convergence rates and reduce training losses. Furthermore, our research indicates that the RCT network learns to make more meaningful representations than its unmodified counterpart.

Utilizing electrical impedance tomography (EIT) for damage detection in materials has gained significant interest over recent years.  However, the interpretation of EIT data remains a challenge, particularly in identifying precise damage characteristics from inversions that yield suboptimal results.  Our study presents an innovative approach to resolving this issue by implementing a genetic algorithm to optimize an explicit model, effectively determining location and dimensions of delaminations.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of a simple circuit and EIT system for real-time damage monitoring in smart composite materials.  Although this approach introduces a phase between voltage and current due to the EIT equipment, our study develops a mathematical formula to convert measured resistance into exact damage locations and sizes.  Moreover, this model allows for damage monitoring without the need for tomographic reconstruction, facilitating direct EIT data interpretation and real-time activation of embedded functional layers through circuitry that connects the sensing and functional layers of the material.

We've successfully solved a significant problem from the theory of homogeneous dynamical systems by characterizing the subgroups of $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$ that allow for a reduction to a point. This solution involves the study of parabolic and hyperbolic elements. Specifically, the pairs of these elements generate specific distributions, known as the Schwinger parameters, and interestingly, the simplest combinations of these elements yield the most complex, non-algebraic results. As a side exploration, we've also considered combinations of elliptic elements and their associated results, which, in contrast, are the most straightforward.

A key challenge in robotics is learning effective behaviors from examples and guidance. Robots can learn behaviors from demonstrations, but these are often insufficient due to variations in execution and equipment. Moreover, demonstrating optimal performance can be complicated and costly. To overcome these challenges, we propose a model-free reinforcement learning approach that utilizes both demonstrated performance and binary side information during execution. Tested on complex, real-world robots for basic locomotion tasks on a differential drive robot and quadruped robot, and a flying drone, our approach efficiently optimizes policies using only binary feedback. Notably, it requires significantly fewer trials than reinforcement learning alone, making it feasible to optimize behaviors with binary side information.

This study explores the capabilities of a geometric framework for a Euclidean space, demonstrating how various tools can be utilized when working with tensor tensors. Key features examined include the effects of space deformation on tensor components, the rate of change of mixed-index tensor values along curved paths, and further related concepts.

A theoretical model, where the standard model is connected through higher-dimensional space to a flavor-changing scalar within a three-dimensional spacial volume. The model predicts that the scalar should be unstable and quickly decay into two photons. The model's characteristics are constrained by experiments, particularly those at the Large Hadron Collider, including searches for the scalar produced in association with the large Hadron Collider. The model's lifespan of the scalar is determined by the size of a specific threshold, which dictates when it would decay. If this threshold is set to a certain level, the scalar could survive until it leaves the detector and even be found as minimal bending trajectories in a muon spectrometer. The model proposes three theories to explain why the scalar would have an unexpected longevity. One suggestion suggests that new physics protects the scalar from decaying, thus increasing its lifespan. Another suggestion suggests that an anomaly in General Relativity causes the scalar to behave differently. A final suggestion suggests that the scalar is affected by its movement through spacetime.

The COVID-19 pandemic forced educators and learners around the globe to adapt to remote learning through remote education technologies. However, the adverse effects of remote learning on students' ability to keep up with the curriculum have been well-documented. This study focuses on examining the significant impact remote learning has had on students' ability to stay on track with their studies during the pandemic. Researchers collected data from 350 participants in Lagos State, Nigeria via surveys and used both descriptive and deductive methods for data analysis. Findings reveal that remote learning adversely impacts students' grades, increases dropout rates and decreases enrollment. Furthermore, it was discovered that remote learning increases dropout rates significantly (β = 1.149, p < 0.05), has a notable effect on enrollment (β = 1.421, p < 0.05) and has a substantial effect on grades (β = 1.428, p < 0.05). As such, this research recommends that necessary infrastructure be provided for remote learning to be more effective.

This research establishes the presence of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-Ward identities within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. As a result, we can extract descendant fields linked to the identity in any number of ways, originating from bosonic fields associated with $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-highest weight module, and their corresponding descendants. These connections enable us to derive an infinite set of additional constraints on the three-point function correlators, supplementing existing constraints from $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-highest weight module. We then demonstrate these relationships using an explicit model. Furthermore, we can generalize this approach to extract descendants of the vacuum and relevant fields in arbitrary ways, derived from a direct sum of multiple $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-highest weight modules. These new relations may help in formulating a comprehensive set of equations sufficient to define the full set of states in any given irreducible $\mathfrak{sl}_3$-highest weight module.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups belong to the class of bi-automatic groups,
implying that they are of type FP_2 as well as having polynomial growth patterns.
Our proof builds upon Ivanov's work on the fundamental group of arc graphs for
hyperbolic polygons, establishing a group presentation from which the bi-automaticity
of Coxeter groups can be derived.

Researchers have investigated the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship hypothesis, specifically focusing on the relationship between an outer event horizon and a naked singularity in a Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black hole. A scalar field was considered in this study. It was determined that a horizon always forms in this scenario. Additionally, the study examined how rare instances of low-entropy states might occur, using both analytical and numerical methods to verify that such states have an extremely low probability. Furthermore, the study found that states with minimal entropy correspond to configurations near the threshold of the naked singularity, where charge and electric potential both oscillate with similar amplitudes, while any deviation from this balance results in the formation of an event horizon.

In this research, we address the limitations of classical logic by incorporating paraconsistent and paracomplete logic into the ZF axioms, specifically allowing for contradictions and undefined statements within the system. By modifying the equality axiom and existential quantifier rule, we create a paraconsistent and paracomplete version of ZF logic, respectively. Furthermore, we analyze the expressiveness of these modified logics and discover that they exceed the capabilities of classical logic. Notably, our research reveals that paraconsistent ZF logic is equivalent to a true theory of proper classes under classical logic, while paracomplete ZF logic can distinguish between sets and classes using an additional formula, also found in true theory books of proper classes under classical logic.

Researchers have long studied human walking patterns and have released various models and measurements for both healthy and injured cases. However, no term could accurately describe the gait cycle of normal, healthy walkers. This study presents new data and analysis based on electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings that reveal new "states" and step frequencies associated with walking. By using high-density pECoG system data from three subjects, researchers were able to analyze the patterns of brain activity during walking cycles. Through clustering methods, they were able to identify distinct "states" and step rates that matched the known phases of a normal gait cycle. This research may have significant implications for the development of more accurate models and interventions for gait disorders.

This paper proposes a new method to estimate the entropy of any probability distribution by leveraging insights from nested sampling. Building upon this, we extend the approach to calculate mutual entropy and condition entropy. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we provide a way to explore entropy surfaces in complex parameter spaces, including necessary conditions for chaotic dynamics in discrete systems. Additionally, this capability can be utilized to study the complexity of the dynamic's attractor in certain dynamical systems. Our method is straightforward to implement and can be integrated with existing nested sampling algorithms, such as the one developed by Foreman-Mackey et al. (2014).

We examine right-angled Artin complexes, focusing on their geometric properties and how they relate to certain groups associated with them. The analysis includes establishing criteria for these complexes to allow for specific group splittings and isomorphisms to sub-structures, with specific attention to those containing a certain diameter. The isomorphism condition is set at a thickness of 2 for certain sub-structures known as circles. A key application of our analysis involves demonstrating that right-angled Artin groups can be expressed as non-trivial free products with amalgamation, using this condition and analyzing how these groups behave under retractions. Additionally, we explore the splittings of these groups using actions on non-positing right-angled buildings, resulting in amalgams of groups.

In the field of machine learning, graph-based methods have gained significant attention due to their ability to reflect the structural information and connectivity patterns present in data. As our ability to collect and analyze high-frequency time series data improves, there is growing interest in clustering algorithms that not only consider temporal statistics but also an intuitive understanding of the underlying connections between variables. While current clustering approaches typically excel at identifying linear relationships, they often lack the flexibility and efficiency required for real-world applications involving large datasets. To address this limitation, we present a new framework called Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity Estimation (DICE), which leverages the power of low-rank representations to efficiently process and analyze complex time series data. By integrating cutting-edge representation learning techniques with a highly scalable efficient variance explanation method, DICE can not only capture both direct and indirect connectivity patterns but also adapt dynamically to changing data trends. Our comprehensive evaluations demonstrate the exceptional performance and consistency of this approach across multiple datasets and reporting times, while its modular design allows for seamless deployment in real-time applications.

The study investigates various phylogenetic networks generation methods, 
examining how each method produces networks with similar structural characteristics. 
Existing research highlights specific properties of the generated networks, 
such as the frequency of tree topologies, but a more in-depth quantitative analysis 
is lacking. This study H2O quantifies network similarity using the Schwartzberg index, 
allowing a more comprehensive comparison of network structures. Our findings suggest 
that certain network characteristics are consistent with specific phylogenetic 
networks generators, yet some other features are not clearly linked to any 
particular method. This study also reveals that the H2O index can be employed to 
investigate the phylogenetic networks properties.

This project demonstrates our findings as a supplementary material to the primary
research. As often occurs in the area under investigation, multiple algorithms
have been tested to accomplish the intended objective. This conclusion
 outlines the
   project's outcomes and provides
 a specific criterion for
  selecting an optimal algorithm.

Restoring a complex, high-dimensional correlation structure within a set of variables is a critical component in many advanced Bayesian methods for data analysis. This task can be broken down into two essential sub-tasks: finding the diagonal elements and off-diagonal components of a covariance matrix. While sampling methods effectively address the diagonal components, a more efficient approach is sought after, particularly for scenarios involving large datasets commonly associated with medium to low signal-to-noise ratios. Various techniques exist to solve the factorization problem, but most are limited to moderate dataset sizes due to their requirement of inverting sub-matrices. Our novel high-order GPU-accelerated factorization (HIGUF) method overcomes these limitations by applying an iterative approach that significantly reduces the computational load and allows the technique to be applied to larger problems.

We develop a comprehensive theoretical framework to analyze the behavior of particles moving through two-dimensional scattering environments. This framework is particularly useful in extracting the linear coefficients of particles' energy deposition eigenchannels. The theory is derived from fundamental principles and can yield the coefficients of eigenchannels using both classical trajectories and quantum mechanical methods. As a result, our framework enables researchers to understand and measure the particles' energy deposition behavior in complex systems. This framework has been applied to scattering systems exhibiting both bound states and anomalous resonance behavior.

Recent theoretical predictions have suggested that an Anderson topological conductor, a two-dimensional analog of a topological insulator, can be found in a randomly disordered honeycomb lattice. Our study provides a comprehensive examination of this model across its entire parameter range using both numerical and analytical methods. Through detailed calculations of the spectral statistics, level quantization, and edge mode localization length, our numerical results confirm the existence of disordered Anderson topological conducting phases. Through first-principles calculations, our findings reveal that these topological phases can be reliably observed despite a significant level of disorder. Furthermore, our numerical and analytical results identify two new types of disordered topological phases, alongside two known kinds of disorder-induced topological phases, including one where the edge modes wind around a specific point. Lastly, our findings show that non-diagonal disorder plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the topological phases by suppressing the localization of edge modes.

The conventional view of linear cutting edges in categories requires objects to have finite composition, but this limitation can be overcome by employing localizable categories, as proposed by Borceux and Combe. This paper presents the fundamentals of localization within additive categories and explores the connection between localized categories and multi-linear cutting edges, as described by Street. Furthermore, it presents a new finding: the category of modules over an algebra can be viewed as having multi-linear cutting edges if and only if the underlying category of vectors has finite composition.

We examine a specific scenario within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, where the mu parameter is set to approximately half the Higgs boson's mass and the CP-violating phase of the $\mu$ parameter is positioned at or near $k\pi$, with $k$ being an integer. This particular configuration leads to a significant reduction in the number of independent CP phases within the scalar sector, potentially inhibiting the occurrence of charge and color breaking minima. As a result, the minimum at the electroweak scale remains dominant. We investigate the conditions under which the Higgs potential possesses a dominant electroweak minimum and assess the associated lifetime. Furthermore, we analyze the capability to produce a Higgs boson through bound states of three top quarks and determine the minimum value of the $\mu$ parameter for which this process can generate a sufficient number of Higgs particles. This proposed scenario is limited to very specific ranges of model parameters and might account for the matter-antimatter asymmetry observed in the universe.

Recently, new research has expanded upon the traditional linear generalized additive models for dependent data, though currently, there is a lack of developed methods for testing these models when accounting for spatial dependencies and the data's inherent correlation. This paper proposes innovative testing methods to assess linearity within a non-parametric model that incorporates autoregressive features, considering both dense and sparse spatial configurations. We establish theoretical properties for the linearity test statistics under specific scenarios, including fixed space parameters, a notable property of our research is its robust performance in various spatial configurations, as demonstrated in the accompanying simulation results. Additionally, a real-data example is analyzed to further support the methods proposed.

Recent research has identified multiple equivalent mathematical formulations that can be effectively tackled by machine learning models, such as Graph Neural Networks, through the integration of declarative models and networks. This approach enables significant improvements in solution quality and runtime for various optimisation and inference tasks. Although some limitations remain with current methods, they do not fully capitalise on key features of optimisation problems, including their objective functions and constraint structures. To address this, we propose an innovative framework that combines a neural optimisation approach with other prominent mathematical formulation techniques. We focus on Network Constrained Generation and Quadratic Knapsack Recovery as example applications and evaluate the performance of our method on both synthetic and real-world data sets. We observe that our framework outperforms alternative methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency for both problem types, with notable gains achieved over specialized models like GNNs and ANNs. To further validate the advantages of our approach, we conduct additional experiments on other problem classes such as Node Classification and Node Embedding.

We present a computational framework for relocation events, as well as the motility and dispersion of cells, using an interface based framework. This framework is particularly useful for cellular systems where cells are not supported by a supervening domain. We exemplify our approach with a multi-cellular interface based formulation that incorporates an array of interdependent features: cells that leave the domain, vary in position, transfer proteins from donor to target cells, and leave behind secreted agents. The formulation utilizes a front-tracking method to define cell geometry and employs a stabilized level set to mark cell boundaries. We present a discretized formulation for the cell system, including methods for locating target cells and efficient solution techniques for the movement of proteins on lipid membranes. The proposed framework is flexible, extensible, and provides a robust foundation for more complex cell models.

The primary method to prevent money laundering in a physical bank is a thorough transaction monitoring system, typically implemented by a dedicated team of investigators known as compliance officers or through automated pattern recognition algorithms. In contrast, there is no equivalent compliance mechanism in place on a public blockchain, as its design prioritizes decentralization and censorship resistance over transaction monitoring. Consequently, researchers are actively investigating ways to develop transaction monitoring systems for cryptocurrency users, with the goal of identifying and flagging money laundering activities. This paper presents a newly compiled dataset, consisting of 344 currency trails associated with large-scale Bitcoin money laundering transactions, analyzed in the context of the historic Bitcoin laundering scandals. By making this dataset available to researchers, we aim to facilitate the development of efficient transaction monitoring systems, capable of accurately identifying suspicious Bitcoin users based on their spending patterns. Our initial research, utilizing the Komodor algorithm, discovered that many cryptocurrency laundering transactions adhere to a structured and predictable structure, characterized by a bipartite cycle graph with distinct "currency trails" forming individual compartments within the transaction cycle. Our proposed algorithm can identify these trails efficiently, utilizing localized graph optimization techniques to minimize an established compliance function that quantifies the difficulty of achieving a particular currency trail given starting and ending amounts and a specified number of hops.

A novel approach has been discovered to overcome the limitation of previous learning-tolerant computations, which involved inserting extra fault checks. Our method allows for the elimination of these unnecessary fault checks. By utilizing a reinforcment learning framework, we can determine the most effective check sets needed to identify and correct any single error, thereby making our general approach more efficient in terms of both time and memory usage.

In the two-cavity quantum metrology setup, we studied the precision of measuring the interaction between the cavities using coherent states as input. Surprisingly, even a small amount of spontaneous emission significantly improves this precision by a notable margin, with an up to 50% enhancement achieved, far exceeding the typical 3 dB improvement seen elsewhere. This optimal enhancement occurs when the coupling rates for the emitted photons are widely different, allowing a 50% improvement over the case where the rates are equal, which corresponds to a quantum enhancement beyond the standard quantum limit.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron associations in 200 GeV/A $d$+$Au$ and Au$+$Au collisions, featuring numerous midrapidity direct photons accompanied by hadrons within the forward hadron spectrum. Results show that the average hadron transverse distance from the direct photon significantly differs between data and theoretical models. Specifically, CRQ and HYJET models fail to accurately reproduce the observed association patterns in Au$+$Au collisions, whereas they overproduce the data in $d$$+$Au collisions. Additionally, the energy loss of hadrons is found to be energy-dependent, with higher energy hadrons exhibiting increased loss, contradicting the field-theory-based JETSCAPE model's findings.

This paper explores the concept of the Smarandache multiplication of digits, specifically focusing on digits that are summed together. Let 'a(n)' denote the smallest positive integer 'k', such that the product of the sums of 'n' consecutive integers starting from 'k', all calculated with their respective digits, equals 'n'. The initial values of 'a(n)' for 'n' from 1 to 150 are listed in a table, along with the corresponding starting values 'a(1)', 'a(2)', and 'a(3)'.

Network noise and network variability are well-known network phenomena that have significant impacts on network performance. These include unexpected events like packet loss, latency increases and jitter, as well predictability issues arising from limited bandwidth in shared networks. Research into these effects has primarily occurred in the context of network management, as good understandings of noise and variability are crucial for the successful design and operation of cloud services. In fact, current research indicates variability should be treated as a vital resource that must be taken into account to ensure reliable scalability. This paper delves deeper into noise and variability as fundamental aspects of network behavior, and develops simple analytical models to explore their influence on multi-node application scalability. These models can aid in predicting how network noise and variability will shape the performance and efficiency of multi-node applications as they expand.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with applications in various fields, and this paper proposes a new approach to handle the contextually linear bandits scenario in a distributed manner. In this scenario, multiple agents make decisions in a contextual linear bandits setting and aim to improve upon the standard result by taking advantage of the fact that they are not competing against each other. We present an algorithm that operates in an asynchronous and communication-efficient manner. The proposed algorithm achieves a slightly worse contextual linear growth rate of the regret when the context dimension is high, and a square root rate in the number of features when the context dimension is low. This performance can be compared to the non-contextual distributed linear bandits scenario, where the standard result is a square root rate in all parameters. We also outline directions for improving the current approach and discuss the contextual linear growth rate of the regret more deeply.

Over the past year, remote working has become widespread due to lockdown measures. 
Our research examined how working from home affects teams utilizing the Scrum framework in Britain. 
We studied 41 teams utilizing the Scrum framework and analyzed factors that influence its success or failure during remote working. 
Our findings indicate that working from home can impede Scrum's success due to difficulties in meeting face-to-face, providing real-time feedback, and maintaining motivation during projects. 
However, when lockdowns ease, teams should be able to regain the benefits of Scrum with returning in-person working conditions. 
Working from home also varies among individuals, with some finding it easier to work without the distractions found in office settings. 
We found that teams' ability to adapt to challenges posed by lockdowns played a key role in their ability to complete projects when using the Scrum framework. 
Finally, our research reveals that working from home can actually boost projects in certain circumstances, including when teams are able to break projects down into manageable parts and stay motivated by sharing their progress with others.

This study examines how event shape engineering can influence the particle production patterns and fluid flow at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically for Pb-Pb collisions at a energy level of 2.76 TeV. By combining measurements of the average transverse momentum with elliptic flow for various types of particles, researchers discovered that these patterns are largely unaffected by initial fluctuations, and instead align with predictions made by hydrodynamic models. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the sensitivity to the initial shape of the collision zone is significantly reduced at this higher energy level.

This paper introduces the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform (QLCST),
which incorporates both matrix-valued functions and a non-quadratic time-scaling
factor. The QLCST possesses beneficial properties, including an inversion formula
and various inequalities. Furthermore, we develop time-frequency atoms (TFAToms)
based on QLCST, establishing both Heisenberg's inequality and a logarithmic
inequality (LINQ) in the context of QLCST. Additionally, we introduce the QLCST
Stein-Tomasi's interpolation inequality (STINQ) and drawing from TFAToms and TFIS,
obtain the quaternion Calder\'on-Zygmund singular integral operator (CZSO) on
$L^{p}$ spaces ($1\le p<\infty$).

This study quantifies the extremal GDoF advantage of optimal power control methods over the commonly used binary power control approach in interference networks, with $O(\sqrt{K})$ representing this benefit for $K$ users. A combination of an upper bound derivation, rooted in a hypothetical network state, and corresponding constructive techniques has yielded the extremal GDoF behavior under maximum power settings, both when limited to binary power states and when freely optimized, thereby validating the upper bound. A pivotal result, establishing the general scalability of the extremal GDoF settings, is proven, which subsequently enables the direct extension of these findings to multi-cellular and heterogeneous networks.

This research focuses on multiple time-step integration techniques used in particle-resolved simulations. The study examines the suitable range for the ratio of simulation time steps between particles and fluid, and determines how this ratio is influenced by the friction coefficient during collisions. Furthermore, it investigates the impact of time-step ratios on key simulation results, including the critical velocity, by varying the properties of particles such as their stickiness and density.

This article will present a proof of a mathematical identity. The given proof establishes an infinite number of integer pairs, $a$ and $b$, for which the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ is divisible by 7 but not 49. Furthermore, this proof will have implications on the infinite number of whole number solutions to the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$.

This paper presents a mathematical model of a one-legged hopping robot moving on a surface that deforms under its weight. We derive the equation of motion for this system, solve it numerically, and compare results for different ground stiffness values. Furthermore, we propose using optimal control to find a more efficient way for the robot to hop by minimizing losses due to friction, testing various strategies in simulation.

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of air, liquid, and solid phases in liquid suspension, there's been little focus on understanding how air-liquid interfaces behave in isolation. In this study, we introduce a new phenomenon where air circulation patterns emerge within an electrically charged droplet due to changes in its surface tension caused by different gases in the surrounding environment. When the droplet is exposed to an air environment and subjected to a sufficiently strong electric field, we observe the formation of a rotating layer of aerosols, which contains a distinct counter-rotating circulation pattern within the droplet. This phenomenon is demonstrated experimentally and validated through computational modeling, which shows that the interaction between the droplet and its environment plays a crucial role in determining when and how the formation of an aerosol layer occurs.

Many individuals struggle with this due to a lack of practice in applying the law of double negation, which states that two consecutive negations cancel each other out.  Therefore, the goal of this work is to create a practice dataset for natural language processing (NLP) systems that encourages them to accurately process negations when generating answers to questions.  To achieve this, a method is proposed where two descriptions of an image are used: one with an additional negation, and answers to those questions are then modified to test the model's ability to disregard the extra negation.  As a result, a dataset was created consisting of over 10,000 carefully annotated records depicting everyday scenes, along with a straightforward process to generate additional negations.  Within this framework, answering certain types of questions relies on the model's ability to disregard the extra negation, and it was found that a model pre-trained on existing data and fine-tuned to a specific task performed below chance when confronted with unanswered questions of this type.  However, it was also demonstrated that incorporating the additional negation into the input allows the model to learn the relationship between negations more efficiently, and it performed significantly better than a baseline approach where models are trained to disregard a single negation, namely the CONDAQA dataset.

Compositional representations, organized by hierarchies, have long been utilized in various fields to facilitate human understanding and communication. Here, we offer an overview of recent advancements in computational hierarchies across diverse information domains. A key trend in these frameworks is the integration of deep learning methods to automate the generation of hierarchical structures. To access this resource effectively, we present four scalable information processing frameworks focused on computing hierarchies in natural language, visual data, auditory information, and text-based networks. Finally, we discuss promising directions for future research in this field.

Quantum annealing's effectiveness can be influenced by sudden quenching, a technique outside traditional QA limitations. Using a sudden quench within an exact cover problem framework, we investigate how quenching affects the computational complexity of the problem and its quantum annealing solution. By analyzing the spectral properties and quantum annealing interval, we find that certain subcases, inherently easy subcases, can become intrinsically difficult subcases through sudden quenching. Furthermore, we observe that the quantum annealing behavior can be influenced by the quenching width, independent of the classical computational complexity.

In many industrial applications, execution traces are often recorded during system operation, but they usually contain unnecessary repetitions of state transitions that hinder efficient analysis. A common approach is to simplify these traces by realigning them after each event, however, this can be computationally costly for large-scale systems. Our research proposes a less resource-intensive method of introducing alignment points during system execution, allowing for the evaluation of multiple, smaller scenarios against their intended specifications. By utilizing infix and post-fix generalizations of the previous line-based approach, we develop an algorithm to identify the minimal number of required alignment points to ensure overall conformance. This method ensures that the combined result of processing these scenarios will conform to the same level of expectation.

Researchers investigated the infinite-layer nickelate LiNiO2's structure, electronic properties, and symmetry using a two-band model. By applying various screening mechanisms to the f-electrons, they discovered that only strong screening led to density functional theory-like results and allowed for a pairing interaction between holes. Strong screening required significant charge transfer from the 3d to the 5f electrons, altering the ground state from 5d1 to 5f1. The strong screening required to achieve pairing resulted in an increased charge transfer gap and reduced hybridization between 5f and 6s electrons, explaining the previously observed unoccupied 5f-manifold in photoemission spectra for lithium nickelate.

This research examines the long-term behavior of non-cutoff Boltzmann equations in three-dimensional space under the influence of a weak vertical phase blending. The study focuses on hard potentials and requires minimal assumptions about the initial data. The analysis demonstrates exponential decay towards a Maxwellian state when the initial data is a small perturbation of a Maxwellian, as well as polynomial decay for more general initial data. The proof relies on establishing decay properties of the Landau equation with cutoff Boltzmann collissions, combined with dispersion mechanisms in the whole space. The resulting decay rates are believed to be optimal based on existing research.

We used sea surface images captured by the European Space Agency's EnMAP and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Cross-track Infrared Sounder during the same date to analyze the work of Cox and Munk from 1964, a foundational study on wave-slope statistics. The models proposed by Cox and Munk 1964 were validated using modern satellite imagery, confirming their accuracy within the limits of visible light. Furthermore, we calculated the models' resolution limit using a mathematical calculation of the Cox and Munk retrieval algorithm, revealing how the models become inaccurate for wave heights exceeding approximately 0.5 meters. This is due to the models producing a distribution of slopes beyond what's physically possible. Although Cox and Munk's wave parameters can be accurately measured using optical satellites for conditions within their limits, this is not the case for microwave-based wind speed estimates. The discrepancy arises due to the influence of long-tailed kinetic energy spectra and the resulting flattening of angular wave slope distributions, which ultimately causes a discrepancy between the models and the physical parameters of the sea.

When designing a large-scale software system, a crucial step is thoroughly testing the system to ensure optimal functionality. One effective method to test the system involves using system-level test cases, which verify the correctness of the overall architecture. However, as software systems grow in complexity, selecting an optimal order to execute these test cases becomes a challenging task. This paper aims to address this challenge by proposing an algorithm to find an ideal test case execution order based on the system's architecture, represented as a directed graph. The proposed algorithm can be run in parallel on multiple processors to efficiently handle large-scale software systems, significantly reducing the time required to determine an optimal test case execution order.

This study examines the impact of COVID-19 on public sentiment analysis by
investigating the emotional undertone of people's opinions during the pandemic,
with a specific focus on China. A new dataset, called MicroCor, is introduced
to address the limitation of existing benchmarks that were not designed for
social emotions. Unlike traditional sentiment classification, this study aims
to identify a range of emotions including urgency, fear, sadness, anger,
calmness, and determination. Two experimental protocols are conducted, first
manually labeling a subset of emotions and then automatically transferring
them to the entire dataset. A thorough analysis of the dataset and the influence
of emotional labels are explored. Additionally, multiple classification
algorithms, both trained and using pre-trained word embeddings, are evaluated
to determine the effect of different embedding methods, the importance of
data balance, and the effect of label quality.

Initially, the interlayer tunneling model was proposed to be a straightforward interpretation of the mechanism behind cuprate superconductivity. However, the latest data indicates that electron interactions in cuprates do not follow this theory. Our analysis reveals that including the charge density wave structure at both layers could reconcile the unusual spectral features; yet, our findings show that this would eliminate the interlayer coupling term responsible for normal conductivity along the c-axis in cuprates.

Research indicates recent data from gravitational waves and neutrinos may imply the sound speed in dense matter could exceed the predicted maximum for massless particles, raising concerns about the consistency of nuclear physics with the existence of compact stars with high masses. This development triggers renewed investigations into the sound speed in dense matter, particularly how it might vary with density, without breaching the relativistic constraint of not outpacing light speed. Our study delves into analyzing the sound speed in matter that could exist within neutron stars, utilizing both non-interacting and interacting particles, including neutrinos, and considering dense matter that lacks quarks, is saturated, or contains three types of neutral baryons, quarks, and hyperons. The implications of these findings on the compatibility of nuclear physics with the existence of compact stars are then examined.

For any algebraic structure, specific rules or identities may be present that are characteristic. To study these structures, it's common to use presenting pairs, which consist of a structure and a set of defining equations. Presenting pairs provide a uniform way to represent algebraic structures and enable the application of computational techniques, such as Tseitin encoding, to analyze their properties. The ability to translate one presenting pair into another while maintaining the underlying structure's presenting nature is essential for comparing and contrasting different presentations. In the case of algebraic trees with disordered labels, we introduce a novel method to achieve this translation, specifically a type of reverse operation for certain presenting pairs, and use this to establish the uniqueness of their algebraic variety.

We've developed a new set of compressed displacement number states and investigated their properties under high compression conditions. Comparing them to their unconditioned counterparts, we found that the 'compression' and 'displacement' conditions work together to enhance the macroscopic characteristics of number states, making them suitable for creating robust quantum superpositions via interference. Furthermore, we demonstrated that these compressed states closely resemble the Gaussian number states used in Gouyet space, while being distinct due to their position within the Hilbert space and their ability to maintain quantum fluctuations at level $\hbar$ rather than $\hbar/2$.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems, where movements occur across the midplane due to gravitational forces. The VSI's ability to mix material within the disk, particularly in facilitating a mixing process between dust and gas, is investigated through computational modeling. The retrograde motion of VSI is capable of influencing the growth of dust structures, as well as modifying factors that limit VSI activity, such as the wavelength of oscillations. The interaction between dust structures and VSI, can lead to altered mixing efficiencies depending on the size of formations, with different outcomes resulting from expansions or contractions of these structures, respectively. The VSI's impact on formations is limited to specific distances, with different retrieval times of these structures from gas occurring at various points across midplanes, particularly as they relate to the development of VSI in different phases of planetary disk formation.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a specific type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time. We have established a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in three-dimensional Ricci flows that exhibit uniform scalar curvature endomorphisms. This result is particularly useful as it enables us to prove that the ends of certain 3D parabolic ends are diffeomorphic to R^3.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training to neural network appliances have facilitated the adoption of backdoors that operate effectively across different updates and models. In a significant breakthrough, researchers devised an innovative technique called the 'global mean pool' (GMP), which facilitates such persistent backdoors by targeting the mean pooling layer. However, the limitations of GMP become apparent when considering scenarios involving multiple updates or models, as it exclusively focuses on the mean features and renders the backdoor trigger fragile. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the concept of competitive synthesis (CS), which creates intricate foreground images containing both the backdoor trigger and target class features. Through a novel technique called the 'mean shift group convolution' (MSGC), we modify the backdoor trigger to ensure that its mean features align with those of the target class. Our refined approach, which we term the 'competitive backdoor' (CBA), establishes the state-of-the-art achievement in terms of stability under multi-update or multi-model scenarios when utilizing the GMP targeting the mean pooling layer.

Researchers are interested in determining global parameters of gravity through observations, particularly the Post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which reflects general relativity's prediction of two gravitating masses carrying space curvature. This study investigates the impact of $\gamma$ uncertainty on astrometric measurements, such as parallaxes and proper motions, using data similar to Gaia's. Analyzing linear and quadratic effects of $\gamma$ uncertainty on these measurements via gravitational metric theories deviations, researchers discovered an effect where extra parallax signal arises from observing errors increasing with distance from the source, and motion apparent on the sky results from the flow of geodesics influenced by $\gamma$ and $\Omega$ uncertainty, and potentially $\Omega$'s uncertainty and possible multiplexing of $\gamma$ and $\Omega$ with other variables affecting astrometry. Considering the expected $\gamma$ uncertainty from combining Gaia's data with Planck's cosmic microwave background data, calculations indicate the impact of $\gamma$ uncertainty on the average residual dispersion of Gaia's parallax data and proper motion data is about one microarcsecond and approximately four times one microarcsecond, respectively, and will be a significant component of the total residual dispersion in both cases. This study also provides formulas and calculations showing the impact of $\gamma$ and $\Omega$ uncertainty on the estimation bias of astrometric metrics, and how the expected bias in the estimated $\varpi$ and $\mu_\ast$ due to $\gamma$ and $\Omega$ uncertainty

We have developed an efficient method for simplifying complex systems by finding a less complex version that still behaves similarly to the original. This method uses a large amount of data about how the system works. We can take several shortcuts: using fewer variables to describe the system and taking advantage of any natural relationships already present in the system. By combining these approaches, we end up with a much simpler version of the original system that still gives reliable results. This method works for a wide range of complex systems, including those that follow specific mathematical patterns, as long as we have enough data about how they behave. We used several examples and real-world data to show that our method produces accurate results and can be very effective when given limited amounts of information.

We investigate an $f(R)$ gravity model with a specific functional form, 
$bR^2/R_c\left(R_\ast\right)$, where $R_\ast$ represents the conformal curvature scalar, 
and parameters $b$ and $R_c$ define the model. By analyzing this model in a 
conformal frame, we find that it can describe a self-boosting soliton, 
characterized by an $R\to\infty$ behavior that represents dark energy in its 
solitonic state. This phenomenon arises due to a nonlocal self-interaction of 
the curvature scalar. In the high-curvature regime, the $f(R)$ model is 
equivalent to $\Lambda$-CDM with a cosmological constant related to $R_c$, and 
thus avoids the well-known pathologies associated with $f(R)$ theories. 
Nevertheless, a direct transformation of perturbations between frames reveals 
that $f(R)$ gravity fails to pass the cosmological tests due to the growth 
problem of structure formation. This failure can be mitigated by choosing a 
specific value of the parameter $b\approx 10^5$, allowing for a stable 
existence of solitons and damped oscillations around this state.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning model inference from bad actors who try to alter the model's output through targeted attacks. In contrast to previous studies that focused on defending against trying to crack the encryption or learn about the training data, our work specifically targets the issue of preventing adversaries from manipulating the model inference output. We identify two critical obstacles in applying existing private inference techniques: the necessity for the encoder to trust both the server and the client, and the high computational cost of secure computation methods. To address these challenges, we develop an optimized framework called SIMC, which leverages simple operations such as addition and comparison, in combination with an existing secure computation protocol. By doing so, we significantly reduce the cost of security from linear to logarithmic. Extensive tests demonstrate that our proposed method is practically efficient and, with only a slight performance decline, robust against various known targeted attacks.

The dynamics and formation of galactic disks are influenced significantly by the distribution of dark matter, a phenomenon that can be observed and studied efficiently at long wavelengths. Using fast radiotelescopes like FAST, researchers can achieve precise insights into this interaction even with small, angularly sized telescopes. Incorporating the data collected by FAST into the broader catalog of radiotelescopic sources in the M101 galaxy group, researchers were able to identify previously uncharted features including small, isolated HI clouds, a large-scale HI tunnel spanning around 10 kiloparsecs, and a prominent HI tail extending from the galaxy NGC 5477. The HI tunnel and tail are likely shaped by the gravitational dynamics between the galaxy and its surrounding matter, a phenomenon that may also be present in similar cosmic settings such as the M51 galaxy group and the Milky Way itself.

To maintain efficiency in Answering Questions without any Answer Choices (Open-Answer), many systems rely on Multiple-Choice answers (Closed-Answer) as a shortcut. While this strategy can be effective, simply copying Closed-Answer systems for Open-Answer can result in low-quality answers that do not fully meet the demands of Open-Answer. To improve this, we propose two key ideas: (1) Incorporating a diverse range of knowledge from answer-candidate snippets rather than relying on a single source of information; and (2) Using a combination of answer-candidate-based knowledge and extra information through a two-stage process that includes both rough selection and careful verification. Furthermore, to better utilize the semantic meaning of these knowledge sources, we introduce three local graph operations that allow query and answer-candidate-specific subgraphs to exchange information. Built upon an existing powerful Commonsense Question-Answering model, our system called Co2CaQA sets a new record-high performance of 54.9 F1 on the Commonsense QA dataset (TacoQA).

The presence of compounds such as water, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide in the nucleus of a comet leads to various processes that produce many molecular species, including H3O+, CO2+ and CO+. Understanding the composition of the comet nucleus and the activities occurring within it can be facilitated by analyzing the spectrum of these molecular ions. While often visible as bright spots in a comet's spectrum, the signals from these ions are typically not strong and require in-depth analysis using the comet's movement across the sky to resolve their wavelengths into finer details. This approach results in a composite spectrum representing oxygen-containing species such as water, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide. Unfortunately, existing research has not established a comprehensive link between the abundances of these major volatile substances and the detected molecular ions, particularly those of H3O+, CO2+ and CO+. Furthermore, the current database of cometary absorption spectra is incomplete, limiting the range of compounds that can be accurately identified. This study gathers and compiles publicly available cometary spectra for references that can guide absorption spectrum modeling, ultimately contributing to the development of comprehensive composite cometary spectra.

Given a finite collection of rectangular regions within a global field, we are tasked with finding two rectangles from this collection that do not overlap but together cover the entire collection. This problem is considered a significant instance of a more complex challenge known as the sums of rectangles problem. While recent research has made substantial strides in understanding this complex issue, particularly in the case of large, unrelated rectangles, further work remains to be done on cases involving rectangles that are not statistically independent.

The technique of cross-correlating spectra is a highly effective technique for detecting exoplanets, utilizing stellar spectral templates to identify subtle patterns. This technique is being used on an increasingly diverse range of objects, from rocky exoplanets to massive gas giants, as well as objects influenced by spiral arms, quasi-stellar objects, and active galactic nuclei. However, the presence of abnormal spectral features in some of these sources, including low-spin broad stellar lines, difficult to correlate in some cases, can pose a challenge. We discuss various strategies to effectively address these challenges, including adjusted preprocessing techniques, tailored correlation functions, advanced deconvolution methods, and taking into account the flow of spectra, to aid researchers in overcoming these difficulties.

In the last few years, predictive modeling that considers the relational data of drugs has made substantial progress in tackling complex medical issues. This-paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the topic by: (1) explaining the fundamental concepts and basic principles of relational learning; (2) presenting a unified framework that encompasses prominent relational models; and (3) exploring the applications of these models to drug pair scoring problems, including the prevention of adverse effects, the prediction of the drug's physiological effects and its metabolism. Furthermore, this paper looks at the current challenges in the field and suggests promising avenues for future research.

The provided article introduces an Itô-Wentzell formula tailored to accommodate paths with low regularity, specifically α-almost sure differentiable paths where α exceeds 3, within the context of stochastic differential equations. It also demonstrates connections between this formulation and existing approaches, including fractional smooth paths, and expresses these paths' differentiability properties in relation to the given α.

The primary issue in Federated Learning (FL) is the variation between clients' data, which significantly slows down FL's convergence. This paper presents an innovative approach to tackle this challenge. We integrate Random Walks (RWs) with FL to handle data heterogeneity. Introducing two new algorithms - Stroll FedAveraging (SFA) and Stroll FedDirect (SFdL) - we allow each client to perform a random walk on their data graph to create a more uniform data distribution at the server. Theoretical analysis proves that our methods achieve an infinite data independence assumption mode convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(\max\left\{\frac{1}{\epsilon},1\right\}\right)$, where $\epsilon$ represents the RW error. Experimental results indicate that our algorithms outperform existing algorithms in terms of lower communication rounds and higher accuracy.

Three-dimensional wave-turbulence systems were numerically simulated in a range of scales to investigate the influence of nonlinearity and dispersion. By analyzing energy distribution across noninteracting cubic volumes, researchers in this study found that nonlinearity can be effectively ignored at a certain level, leading to a local equilibrium state. The interaction time and rate were then examined in relation to the level of energy and a generalized exponent was estimated. The results showed that the generalized exponent converges to approximately 3.65, a value that aligns with the predicted Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum for three-dimensional weak turbulence. Furthermore, a more general formula was derived and discussed, allowing for the exploration of similar concepts in other types of wave turbulence systems.

This research examines the impact and versatility of mental health treatment for incarcerated individuals on recivism, utilizing the unique natural experiment provided by French justice system reforms. The effect of mental health treatment on reoffending is assessed, including its variances based on treatment intensity and crime severity. Results reveal that incarcerated individuals who receive mental health treatment have lower rates of reoffending compared to those who do not receive treatment. Lower levels of reoffending are observed for criminals with higher baseline risks of returning to crime. Furthermore, the decrease in recivism is more significant for property crimes than violent crimes. Fostering mental health within the criminal justice system may have both economic and social benefits.

A pervasive challenge in medical image segmentation lies in the lack of sufficient annotated images. Semi-supervised learning techniques that combine existing labeled and unlabeled data have shown promising results for improving classification performance. However, simple aggregation of existing consistency regularization methods is inadequate for improving medical image segmentation due to multiple simultaneous constraints. In this work, we introduce a straightforward yet effective semi-supervised consistency regularization framework, specifically tailored for medical image segmentation. The proposed framework is tested on two widely used datasets, ISIC-18 and PANnD, for segmentation mask prediction. The proposed method significantly enhances prediction accuracy when compared to existing supervised baselines, with substantial improvements of around 5% and 2.5% respectively, with notably reduced computational requirements.

The ATLAS Jet Calorimeter Trigger system on the Experimentally Local Experiment (ELE) side requires a significant upgrade to handle the increased data load from Run 3. This upgrade will involve migrating from Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) based on the Xilinx Virtex-5 series to the non-end-of-life Xilinx UltraScale+ series. However, adapting board design principles and software tools from the older to the newer FPGA series has been a significant challenge due to the notable differences in series architectures. As part of the ATLAS Ele-FPGA upgrade project, the group has designed and fabricated new high-velocity boards utilizing the Xilinx UltraScale+ series, specifically targeting run-time power consumption and achieving the shortest possible latency while adapting to the new FPGA architecture. This project has successfully completed testing and will start replacing older boards at the beginning of Run 3.

This paper presents a new technique for visualization that accounts for
articulated movements. Our method efficiently transforms the shape of a 3D human
model by using a small number of joint parameters and body transformations.
Virtual avatars are effectively manipulated through this approach, allowing
for accurate visualization of human movement in various forms. Our method builds
upon a patch-based reconstruction technique and utilizes a predefined grid of
parameters to transform the model. By optimizing these parameters, our approach
ensures a high-level accuracy in visualization while maintaining computational
efficiency. Our method is particularly useful in applications such as animation,
biomedical visualization, and virtual reality experiences.

A key feature of an artificial intelligence system is its ability to provide interpretable results that outline the reasons behind its decisions. Though the effectiveness of graph neural networks has been proven, understanding how they make predictions based on input data remains a challenge. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach that incorporates local interpretability into a graph neural network, specifically tailored for predicting chemical reactions. Our method not only identifies the reactions that are most likely to occur, but also those with lower probabilities, along with the underlying reasons for the network's classification. To demonstrate the potential of our method, we applied it to a dataset consisting of over 7000 atom shuffling reactions, showing that the reasons it provides are consistent with established chemical reaction theories. Furthermore, we were able to teach the network to make more accurate predictions by targeting specific atoms that it had initially focused on. Our research indicates that the graph neural network is capable of capturing complex patterns in chemical space, akin to the hallmark of chaotic behavior, and our method paves the way for more efficient exploration of this complex landscape.

Consider a scenario with $p$ distinct groups of real numbers, denoted as $\mathcal{P}_1,\dots,\mathcal{P}_p$, and let $Y$ be a random variable that can be represented as a mixture of elements from these groups. The probabilities of this occurrence are given by $w_j$, and the distribution of each group follows the measure $\mu_j$. Our objective is to estimate the average of the parameters of $\mu_j$, denoted as $\theta_j$, and thus form an estimated measure $\delta_n$ to estimate $\theta$, which is a weighted sum of $\theta_j$, with corresponding weights of $w_j$. Under certain technical conditions, we can derive the asymptotic behavior (both weak and strong) of estimators $\theta_{n,j}$ and determine their rate and limit as they converge to average parameters $\theta$. Specifically, this framework can be applied to estimate parameters in a two-group model from the Hansen-Hedberg sampling method, where the HED measure consists of uniformly distributed values within an unknown interval and discrete mass at another estimable point $\theta$. Through a semi-parametric approach, we can achieve more efficient estimation of $\theta$ by incorporating information obtained from the HED measure.

Knowledge tracing is an adaptive learning technique that evaluates a student's current understanding of a subject through analysis of their past academic performance. 
Knowing precisely how well a student knows a topic is vital for suggesting appropriate content for optimization. Multiple knowledge tracing models based on deep learning can be evaluated using `pyKT`, a Python library that offers utility functions and pre-trained models for common deep learning knowledge tracing algorithms.
Algorithms included in `pyKT` are Logistic Regression, LSTM, 1-TCN, and a Logistic Regression variation that takes into consideration student's past performance on similar problem types. The library enables the evaluation of these models in both supervised and unsupervised settings, with the latter including re-initialization and embedding techniques. Performance results from common datasets show the parity of deep learning models to a leading trickled technique. Furthermore, `pyKT` provides a framework for the straightforward incorporation of novel deep learning models.

Given a compact variety $X$ with no singular points, if $P$ is an elliptic differential operator of order $m$, then for any $s\in\mathbb R$, there exists an integer $l\ge 0$ such that for any $s'\in\mathbb R$, the restricted operator $P|_{\perp\mathrm{Im}\,P_{s'-l}}\subset H^{s'}(X,\mathbb C), H^{s'(X,\mathbb C))}$ shares the same closed range as $P$. Additionally, the domain $\perp\mathrm{Im}\,P_{s'-l}$ can be defined as the set of all sections $u\in H^{s'}(X,\mathbb C)$ on $X$ such that the local pairing $\langle u,\phi\rangle$ is an analytic function of $\phi\in H^{s'-l}(X,\mathbb C)^{\infty}$ within a neighborhood of $0$. Notably, this property holds even when $X$ has a sufficiently mild singularity.

Towards completing the notion of verified arguments, the format known as TASTY has been developed. This format can be utilized to represent proof arguments from various sources, including those from the solvers Alt-Ergo, Coq, and multiple SAT solvers, in their native formats. The solver Alt-Ergo produces its own specific format, which has been integrated into the broader Althe system, an extension to Alt-Ergo that is capable of utilizing the TASTY format, offering a more readable and structured representation of proofs. Additionally, the ability to convert proofs into the TASTY format from Althe has been demonstrated.

This research paper proposes a novel framework for a Federated Learning system that utilizes unrestricted model gradient information and introduces an innovative approach called Double-Queue Buffered Asynchronous Aggregation (DBAA). In the traditional FBAA setting, there are several limitations including the requirement of unbiased data and the direct impact of delayed models on the aggregated model. The proposed DBAA approach overcomes these issues by separating aggregation delays from update delays and giving back the benefit of unrestricted gradients. It was discovered that DBAA not only converges but also outperforms the standard buffered asynchronous aggregation method. The results showed an improvement of around 15% in convergence speed when utilizing the DBAA approach.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have been outperforming traditional ASR methods thanks in part to the use of a fine-grained time alignment model, specifically a time iteration unit network. Although these systems achieve top-notch results, the large number of parameters required in their models poses a challenge, particularly when applying them to resources that are scarce. This study explores the potential of employing a less detailed time alignment model in neural ASR transfer scenarios, specifically investigating whether a simpler time iteration unit network can work in conjunction with a transfer-based system to deliver comparable results. Through comprehensive experiments across three language pairs, our research demonstrates the viability of using a coarse time alignment model in cross-language ASR transfer and further improves outcomes via the addition of auxiliary losses in a multi-task learning framework.

The Twitch dataset is composed of nearly 2 million professional gamers represented as a large, complex network, where the connection strength between any two players is determined by their jointly streamed tournaments. This dataset is ideal for assessing novel node embedding techniques on large-scale, real-world networks, specifically those that preserve the proximity of connected nodes and consider the structural roles of nodes within the network. As the first of its kind, the Twitch dataset combines multiple elements from existing benchmarks but on a significantly larger scale.

Our study suggests that any observed interactions between $f_X(1500)$ and the $\rho^0(1450$) resonance could stem from the $f_X(1500)$ resonance feeding into the $\rho^0(1450)$ state, which in turn decays into dipions. Consequently, we conclude that $f_X(1500)$ is not present in the $B\to \pi \pi \pi$ decay data. Furthermore, we estimate the upper limit of the branching fraction for the $B^+\to \rho^0 \pi^+  \to  (\pi^+ \pi^-) \pi^+  f_X(1500)$ decay at the 0.036 level.

We suggest a new "dimension" in physics, representing unseen, real-world properties, and argue that a new particle's validity depends on two conditions: it must be a scalar particle with an extremely low mass scale, and a significant fraction of dark matter must be comprised of primordial black holes. Filling the "dark dimension" would require discovering a new particle with a moderate mass scale, but this contradicts recent findings on stable primordial black matter. If the "dimension" remains closed, the mass scale of new physics could be reached with the next high-sensitivity collider, and we explore possible scenarios within the "dark dimension," including a new particle with a moderately low mass scale, such as the dark photon.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in SAAs and force-fed actuators is introduced, centered on a innovative force observation method called the Transmission Force Estimator (TFE). This approach effectively estimates the transmission force by filtering out the effects of the actuator's series spring using an integral filter, and can use a simplified dynamic model, potentially ignoring the actuator's dynamics, to increase control torque accuracy. The TFE's performance is theoretically validated and supported by extensive simulations and experiments, showing that actuators regulated using this method achieve significant reductions in tracking errors, often by two orders of magnitude, particularly during phases of force control. The algorithm's efficacy is further enhanced by the use of a relatively low-gain filter in TFE, making it less susceptible to noise interference, and by selecting appropriate appropriate transmission force feedback coefficients, and achieving negligible steady-state force regulation errors, and with potential improvements, even better force control accuracy, and potentially series elastic actuator application. A self-driven monolayer of particles can organize into ordered regions called rafts that are separated from each other by disordered areas. This research utilizes a simple model to study the properties of these disordered regions. Through simulations and analytical calculations, we find that the gap width is directly proportional to the viscosity ratio and can be manipulated to observe distinct features. Furthermore, we reveal that the particle density within the gaps follows a unique pattern and that the movement of this pattern can be understood through a specific mathematical framework. Additionally, the viscosity ratio within this pattern is found to be independent of the surrounding rafts and can be defined by a specific threshold value.

Lattice gauge field research has shown that lattice SU(Nc) theory can demonstrate a wide range of phase transitions as the lattice group size increases. This study focuses on understanding the lattice SU(Nc) gauge theory in three dimensions with a range of lattice group sizes, from 2 to 3. Specifically, it investigates the Higgs, confining, and non-singular phases, as well as a new phase called the lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase. This research particularly explores the impact of lattice group representation and on the phases of lattice SU(Nc) gauge theories with mass and strength control over a scalar field. By varying the lattice group from SU(2) to SU(3), it is demonstrated that the lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase can exist independently of the lattice group group size. However, the Higgs phase can be accessed with a fixed lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase, by increasing the cascade of the representation and lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase. This study finds that the lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase is more extensive when using a smaller lattice group group size and a smaller lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase can be accessed with a smaller lattice group group size. This study finds that the lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase is more extensive when using a smaller lattice group group size. By analyzing the lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase in more detail, it is proposed that the lattice SU(Nc) symmetric phase can be understood as a multi-component order

Our novel approach combines Gaussian Process models with Time Difference Learning in a Sparse configuration to create an efficient policy learner for robotics in complex environments. By integrating these components, we address issues of data efficiency and scalability that typically hinder GP TD learning in standalone use. Our method demonstrates improved performance in terms of training time and data efficiency when applied to marine robot guidance, particularly in wide, shallow waters where traditional methods struggle due to varying water currents. Utilizing a second-order value function and difference equation, we optimize the algorithm for data efficiency and feasibility for training before solving the resulting non-linear system using gradient-based techniques. Utilizing a sparse representation allows for substantial computational gains over the typical matrix-based TD learning, while retaining similar data efficiency properties. Utilizing a limited number of GP components further reduces computation while retaining similar data efficiency. Limited training is required with our approach compared to established marine robot guidance techniques, even in variable water conditions.

We observe that the optimal constant-depth linear sorting networks outperform optimal non-degenerate swapping networks by achieving lower element rates. Furthermore, research within this paper reveals the optimal non-degenerate 2-element swapping network circuits for sorting networks of constant depth d for all d between 3 and 10, along with corresponding element rates.
